speechtext: Second report of special committee on reconstruction and reestablishment.-Mr. T urgeon.
(Questions answered orally are indicated by an asterisk.)
Questions

1.	Have the paper mills at Riverbend, Jonquiere, and Kenogami, been shut down?
2.	If so, (a) by whose orders; (b) on what date; (c) for what reasons; (d) for how long?
3.	To whom do these mills belong?
4.	By whom have they been operated?
5.	By whom is the electric power furnished for each of these mills?
6.	Do these mills receive any compensation while shut down? If so, how much, from whom, and for what reason?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
1.	The three mills have been partially shut down on a number of occasions since September 1, 1942, and completely shut down on one occasion.
2.	The partial shut downs were caused by curtailment of power, repairs and holidays.
The Riverbend mill was also shut down at various intervals during the month of January, 1943, and up to February 3, owing to the storm conditions causing car shortages in that area.
On April 7, 1943, the newsprint administrator was notified by Price Brothers & Co. Ltd., that the Riverbend mill had gone out of operation at 10 p.m. on April 6, 1943, and the Kenogami mill at 8 a.m. April 7, 1943, due to a walk-out on the part of the workmen. The Jonquiere mill was similarly shut down. These shut downs lasted until April 26, 1943.
3.	The Riverbend, Jonquiere and Kenogami mills belong to the shareholders of Price Brothers & Co. Ltd.
4.	The Riverbend and Kenogami mills have-been registered with the newsprint administrator as being operated by Price Brothers & Co. Ltd. The Jonquiere mill is operated by the same company.
5.	According to information received from Price Brothers the electric power for these mills is supplied by the Saguenay Power Company and from plants owned by Price Brothers & Co. Ltd.
6.	No decision has yet been reached as to whether the Kenogami and Riverbend mills will be entitled to receive any compensation while shut down and no definite settlement has yet been made with the mills in connection therewith. The Jonquiere mill does not receive any compensation while shut down.

Since no one else has seen fit to do so I should like to direct a question to the attorney general relating to a dispatch appearing on page 4 of the Toronto Globe and Mail of this morning. A former member of this house, an old parliamentarian and a lady with a keen sense of humour, is alleged to have stated in Kenora last night that "she had never met a progressive judge" and that "judges are all political heelers or they would not be judges." I am aware of the parliamentary rules, but I want to say that many of these overworked judges have lost their sons in this war, and I think some statement ought to be made in this connection by the Minister of Justice.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): My attention was directed to this short dispatch just a few moments ago. Certainly it is regrettable that declarations of this kind should be made by or attributed to persons so well known as Miss Macphail, who for a number of years was a member of this house. The statement is as unfortunate as it is unfounded. Declarations of this kind can have no other effect than to diminish the respect of the people for the administration of justice in this country, and as such they are most deplorable. I shall direct the attention of the censors to this dispatch, and see if arrangements cannot be made that publicity will not in future be available for matters of this kind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 22, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, the man-power situation in Canada has been much in the public mind in recent months and has been the subject of considerable debate in this chamber. It has been charged from across the floor that there is a man-power "muddle" in Canada, yet one hears few constructive suggestions which would help the government to improve matters. In my opinion, and I believe the opinion of a great majority of this house, we have the best possible manpower policy that can be devised. I say that having in mind all we are doing to help win this war, our limited population, the vast territory over which this population is spread, there will be widespread agreement with this statement. .
Not very widespread.

Not as far as my hon. friend is concerned, of course. No apology need be made for the selective service programme of Canada. There are and will continue to be labour shortages, emergency conditions will arise which will necessitate emergency measures, but we are engaged in a total war and things cannot be as normal as ' in peace time. In fact if we did not have labour shortages we could not claim to be waging total war. Of course we have a manpower problem in Canada. We will have it for the duration of the war. As our main concern is the provision of adequate fighting forces there must of necessity be improvisation and adjustment of the available forces for work on the home front. Hundreds of thousands of our finest men have joined the

War Appropriation-Labour
navy, army and air force. Thousands of women also are in uniform. We have the greatest combined fighting forces we have ever had in our history.
The strength of our armed forces alone is enough to create a man-power problem on the home front. But in addition we have a huge number of men and women working in our war plants. This naturally has led to shortages in agriculture, mining, fishing and timber operations and in other industries closely associated with our war effort. You cannot take five from ten and still have ten. That is elementary.
Hon. members should keep uppermost in mind the magnitude of our navy, army and air force and the fact that our industrial output and food production is now the greatest in our history. It must be admitted that this is a wonderful achievement by the Canadian people.	.
The leader of the opposition has stated that-and I quote-"the problem of manpower in Canada is the major issue facing the Canadian people." All warring countries have man-power problems and we in Canada are striving to meet our problem in the most effective way.
In a progress report on man-power issued by the office of war information of the United States, No. 1844, there are several paragraphs of interest to us in discussing our situation.
I quote:
Evidence that shortages have been met so far lies in the fact that production has been maintained and increased.
And further:
Mere statement of the main phases of manpower prove it is a national problem of the utmost importance. More advanced over-all programming might have headed off many of the dislocations and difficulties that harass us now-but the solution of man-power problems, it must be emphasized, is almost entirely local, in the hands of every citizen, every community.
I would like the house to note this official view in Washington:
National Service Act or not, man-power problems will be with us throughout the war and after. We will meet them, as we have met those so far, community by community, plant by plant, through better use of workers, training the untrained, by eliminating the causes of wasteful turnover and absenteeism and by working harder for longer hours, up to the maximum of efficient production. Our needs for munitions, essential civilian goods and food will be met, because they must be met, but only by hard and unremitting work.
That is the end of the quotation, Mr. Chairman. I submit in all sincerity that we have been striving since early in the war to grapple with our problems in much the same way as our good friends to the south of us. .
To-day in Canada 5,100,000 men and women out of a total population of 8,720,000 aged 14 and over are in the armed services or at work. That is almost 60 per cent of those aged 14 or over. It is a good record. It is something to be proud of.
I shall lay on the table and request permission to publish in Hansard various statistical tables. One of the most important of them breaks down Canada's total population aged 14 and over. This table shows the distribution of that population by sex, according to those in the armed forces, those at work and those not at work. It gives comparative figures for August, 1939, June, 1941, and January, 1943, the distribution for the last two dates being shown as between civilian employment and war employment. This table will show the house that since the start of the war there has been an increase of about 1,000,000 in the number of persons in our forces and at work; that we have to-day a total of 1,700,000 in the armed services and our war plants and associated industries; that in addition we have
2,100.000	persons in agriculture and essential civilian employment. These groups include 70 per cent of all males in Canada 14 years and over.
Are those figures the result of a survey?

My hon. friend may ask questions when I am through. I shall be quite prepared to answer.
The table further indicates that during the year and a half ended January 30, 1943, there was an increase of 915.000 in the number of persons in the armed forces or war industry. Meanwhile there was a decline of 92,000 in the number of those engaged in civilian employment which largely represents a drain of manpower from work unnecessary in wartime.
Our man-power policy is quite clear. It is to provide the greatest possible number for our armed forces, while at the same time supplying the necessary men and women for our war industries, farms, base metal mines, lumber camps, railways-inland and sea-going shipping.
To meet this problem we have diverted men and women from low to high priority industries, according to their skills and physical strength, without depriving any young men or women in this country from the privilege and honour of serving "voluntarily" in the armed forces of this nation, with the single exception of coal mining.
Because of the great increase in our army of workers we must maintain more of certain civilian services than would otherwise be
War Appropriation-Labour

needed, such as manufacturing, trade, distribution, transportation, communications and construction of homes. But through controls administered by the wartime industries control board, wartime prices and trade board and selective service there has been a sharp drop in the employment of persons engaged in the production and sale of things we can do without until the war is over.
The commendable desire of our young men and women to volunteer for service in the navy, army and air force naturally led to shortages of labour for the jobs at home. These shortages have been added to by the thousands of men called up for service in Canada under the National Resources Mobilization Act. In addition to the drain of man-power into the armed services, the movement of men and women into war plants creates difficult problems with which we are dealing every day.
A year ago-in March, 1942-we placed restrictions on the exodus of man-power from the farms, we also restricted employment of able-bodied men and women in certain occupations by requiring government permits. These controls were tightened in June, 1942, when order in council P.C. 5038 was passed by which among other things and subject to certain conditions, no employer can take any person into employment without notifying a local national selective service office. And in August, 1942, to establish more extensive controls over employment than those in force at the time, the national selective service regulations were enacted by order in council P.C. 7595.
We rapidly expanded our employment office organizations, because that is the very basis of our policy. It consists now of 216 offices and a staff of 4,400 against 75 offices and a staff of 425 in 1940. This will give hon. members some indication of the expansion of the placement machinery under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. On February 1, 1943, in order to amend and consolidate the various orders and regulations affecting manpower we adopted the national selective service civilian regulations as covered by P.C. 246.
On April 2, 1943, we secured authority by order in council 2665 for the compulsory transfer of persons to more essential jobs. The order covers single men 19 to 40 years of age and married men 19 to 25 years of age, the classes designated under the call-up regulations.
Under the authority given to the minister two orders have been made covering transfers from specified industries and occupations. The purpose is to assure that men found not
[Mr. Mitchell.1
fit for military service should do important work at home, not be left in non-essential occupations. These orders are the logical sequence to the system of call-ups for army service in Canada. Men now are to be called for vital civilian jobs to fill in the gaps in our production programme.
As the Prime Minister told the house on May 17, the production of coal officially has been declared a national emergency. A shortage of labour in coal mining has been accentuated by the greatly increased demand for coal in war industries. Last October we arranged to have coal miners receive special consideration for postponement of military service and instructed national selective service officers not to issue any permits for coal miners to seek any other employment. Then we arranged to have coal miners granted leave from the armed services in Canada if they were willing to return to the mines. Subsequently we established the emergency coal production board after full consulation with the national selective service advisory board and the man-power advisory committee of the coal industry. ^
We have issued an order requiring all excoal miners to return to coal mining regardless of their present occupations and are guaranteeing them full employment. We have also, in this same connection, authorized the employment of women in surface operations at the mines.
While ah means of locating ex-coal miners are being used, we should not overlook how much the country owes to the men who have been mining our coal. By their exertions they have done their best not only to maintain coal production of the individual, but to increase it with marked success. In continuing at their hazardous occupation these men are making their greatest contribution to victory. Most assuredly they deserve the nation's thanks. I would like here to appeal to union officers in the coal mining industry to give the government and the people of Canada full support in this grave emergency. We invite cooperation and we need it.
Within the past week, some further measures have been taken for the direction of manpower to essential employment, in the light of present conditions. These are:
Increased control has been taken over the employment of youth .16, 17 and 18 years of age, by making persons of these ages subject to compulsory transfer orders in the same manner as men in the age groups liable for military service.
To provide man-power for fuelwood-cutting operations in view of the threatened fuel-

War Appropriation-Labour
wood shortage for the coming winter, selective service officers have been authorized to give compulsory direction for the employment of men between the ages of 16 and 65 in this work. A similar provision has been made for direction to employment in fishing and fishprocessing, in order to meet the pressing needs of the fishing industry of the maritime provinces and to bolster production of this necessary food.
Following upon representations from the provincial departments of education, provision has been made by amendment to selective service (civilian) regulations to retain in the teaching profession the services of teachers presently employed in schools, colleges, and universities which are not operated for gain. The new regulation forbids the employment of a bona fide teacher in any other occupation without the issuance of a special permit from a selective service officer, which permit will be issued only in accordance with conditions and directions approved by the Minister of Labour.
We have a priority plan for certain munitions industries-assuring that military callups would not adversely affect vital production. Care has been taken to see that then has not been abuse of this arrangement. Ii will be appreciated by the house that the contribution being made to the war effort of Canada by our munitions plants is of a character that will stand tremendously to the credit of our country years after the war is over. We had to keep this in mind while at the same time giving prime consideration to seeing that men were made available for the armed forces. That was our first task and I think it is the demand which was made in this house of members of the official opposition. It is axiomatic, however, that without the necessary munitions of war it would not help to have a large force of fighting men-unless we were to depend on others to supply them with equipment.
We also established a priority list which gave preference to labour needs in base metals and other very essential occupations. The priority arrangement has been the heart of our selective service system.
The question of farm labour has already been discussed in this house. Much ground was covered on June 3 when the house adjourned the regular order of business to deal with the problem. At the time I expressed disappointment that this phase of the man-power problem should be picked out for separate discussion from all others. If we are to use our man-power resources with the
greatest possible efficiency we must look at the problem as a whole and not by individual industries or occupations.
We do not need to be ashamed, Mr. Chairman, of the way we have handled the agricultural phase of our man-power problem. Rather can we feel satisfied with what has been done. Many of the criticisms which have been made during discussions of farm labour have been based on what some hon. member has heard, or on some letter which he has received, or on individual circumstances which have come to his attention.
We must view the agricultural labour problem as a national one, and as part of the total war effort of this country. Also we must appreciate that we can point to a record of achievement all over Canada in farm production which has even exceeded the fondest hopes of my colleague the Minister of Agriculture.
Some hon. members criticize the government because men and women have been allowed to leave the farms for service in the armed forces or to work in war industry. If we had not permitted this exodus from agriculture, the man-power resources of this nation would not have been used anywhere nearly as effectively as they have been used.
Coincident with the drain of man-power from agriculture during each year of the war, production on our farms has continued and is still continuing to soar. This actually represents a great increase in the efficient use of our man-power, when we find fewer people doing more work.
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that older people on the farms have been working harder than ever before. It is true that some farmers have been labouring under the additional difficulty of being unable to secure what new mechanical equipment they may need. It is also a fact that their task has been made harder by many war-time restrictions which they find irksome and annoying. But Mr. Chairman, is not this'evidence of our waging total war? Can any of us escape this, should we want to, if we mean what we say when we ask for an all-out effort? Let us be frank and honest about this question. We should be working harder, we should be tired, we should be working under added difficulties if we truly are engaging in total war. Farmers knowing this have attained a very high standard, one at which we might all well aim.
While my colleague the Minister of Agriculture is more familiar with the detail than I, we find that in this fourth year of war, more dairy products are being raised than
War Appropriation-Labour

ever before, larger numbers of live stock are on farms than ever before, greater flocks of poultry are being kept than ever before.
According to the bureau of statistics "Intentions to Plant Survey", farmers planned this spring to sow more acres to field crops than ever before. It is true that in many areas farmers' plans have been seriously disrupted by the weather, and, regrettable as it is, hon. members cannot hold me responsible for much of the land being under water for the whole month of May.
We will let you off on that.
Thank you, but that is about the only thing you will let me off on.
You always take the credit when there is a good crop.

What our farmers have done is to produce more and more with fewer people. This record of achievement by our farmers, their wives, their children, and their hired men and women will be read some day as one of the glorious chapters in our history. I should like as Minister of Labour to pay special tribute to the hired men and women on the farms. They are too often forgotten in plans for social betterment. Their lot is not an easy one or an exciting one. They are doing a grand war job to-day for this nation.
May I say this to my hon. friends, that when Mr. Churchill gave his rallying call to the British people when they had almost nothing left to fight with but their bare fists, he did not set up a wailing wall but gave them leadership.
That is what we have never had here.

Oh yes, and I think it is proven conclusively by the figures I have given on the farm situation. You cannot expect our farmers, if they are approached in a negative way, to rise to the occasion when a special effort is required, any more than you can expect it of people engaged in any other industry.
Men and women have left the farms by the hundreds of thousands for the armed services and war industries. Those left at home have done and are doing a bigger job than ever.
I have not said these things, Mr. Chairman, to suggest that all is well and that there is no problem on the farm labour front. We know that this problem is great and full of difficulty. But I do implore members of this house to examine and discuss this problem from a
[Mr. Mitchell.!
national viewpoint, and to consider it as part and parcel of the total war effort of this nation.
Neither would I wish it to be inferred from what I have said that we could go on for ever taking more people out of agriculture and still go on producing more and more. We obviously could not. It is more than a year ago since the government took steps to protect the agricultural labour supply by placing restrictions in the way of men and women leaving agriculture for other civilian employment. It was evident at that time that. such restrictions were necessary if our war effort was to be kept in proper balance. The reasons were made abundantly clear by the Prime Minister in his address to this house in March, 1942, on national selective service policy. As we have progressed and have gained experience, amendments have been made to the original order, so that the effectiveness of the agricultural freezing regulations would be increased.
If any hon. member who is a farmer is sceptical about our meaning business in the administration of this feature of our regulations, he might go into an employment office and try to get a permit to leave agriculture. That is the best test, I think, of the effectiveness of the policy. Undoubtedly there has been some evasion of this regulation. Even to-day there will be individual cases of men getting away from the farms when they should have been refused permits. But in the main, this policy has proven effective. It is safe to say that there are thousands of men and women now in agriculture who would not be there now had this regulation not been administered in a resolute way.
In stabilizing labour in agriculture the government had to face the fact that during some periods of the year farm man-power can be more productively employed elsewhere. Our civilian man-power regulations enable a person, under certain conditions, to accept employment in another essential industry when he can be spared from agriculture.
But selective service went further than merely enabling such persons to take other work. It undertook an intensive appeal last fall to all farm workers not needed in agriculture during the winter months to work in other essential industries. In particular they were urged to go to logging, saw mills, coal mines, and base metal mines, where men were urgently needed.

War Appropriation-Labour
This appeal was the first large scale attempt by national selective service to direct manpower from one industry to another. Its success was due, to a large extent, to the excellent cooperation we received from the interested provincial government departments. As a result of it, farm man-power which might otherwise have been relatively idle helped to meet the growing shortage of labour in these other strategic wartime activities.

I would like now to refer for a few minutes to the selective service mobilization regulations affecting agriculture. In March, 1942, these regulations were amended to strengthen the policy of stabilizing employment in agriculture. This amendment incorporated a provision for the postponement of farm workers distinct from the method to be used in granting postponements to all other workers, no matter how high the priority of their work might be.
The new regulations provide that on receipt of an application from a farm worker, the mobilization board was required to grant postponement, "until further notice" unless the board was satisfied that the worker was not essential to agriculture. In other words, the boards must prove that farm workers are not essential whereas in the case of all other workers they themselves have to prove to the boards that they are essential. Essential farm workers get postponement "until further notice", while postponements for all other workers at present are for not longer than twelve months for the first call, and for not longer than six months for subsequent calls.
We freely admit that there have been individual cases decided in such a way as to merit criticism. More might have been done to make clearer to the farmers themselves the significance of the special provisions in the regulations which affected them.

I have mentioned our system of priorities for labour. Classification, I think everyone will agree, is absolutely essential for the allocation of man-power to its most effective uses in the war effort. The minister's authority to classify industries, etc., is exercised by the labour priorities division in the labour supply branch of the Department of Labour. Consultation with the Department of Munitions and Supply and wartime prices and trade board is provided by regular meetings of an informal committee on labour priorities. A carefully worked out analysis of Canadian industries has been prepared as an industrial classification manual by the statistics branch of the Department of Labour. This manual serves as the basis on which industries are selected for designation with respect to essentiality. All industries are given one of four labour priority ratings, "A" meaning very high; "B" meaning high; "C" meaning low; and "D" meaning no labour priority. Occasionally the priority rating of an industry for men is different than for women.
On application to the priorities division and on recommendation of various associations and governmental departments, individual firms are considered by the priorities committee for special ratings. Members of the committee investigate the authenticity of claims and, where justified, the firms are specially named with a rating other than that of their ordinary industrial classification, depending on the proportion of essential production carried on by the firm.
Each local employment and selective service office is provided with, (a), an industrial card index which consists of a card for each industrial classification, showing the labour priority rating for the industry., and in some instances key occupations in the industry; (b) a list of named firms, which includes those establishments and construction projects which are considered individually by the priority committee and are assigned special ratings other than those of the industries under which the firms are classified.
Local offices are advised at once of priority revisions by the labour priorities division, after consultation with interested departments. On receiving an order for labour, local office officials decide the applicant's
War Appropriation-Labour

priority rating by reference to this industrial card index or list of named firms. Available labour is referred to the highest priority vacancy for which it is suitable- or qualified.
The movement of man-power between and within priority groups can be and is being checked by the quarterly employment' survey report. The industrial classification manual is used as the basis for these reports.
There are of course frequent changes in our war production programme, and because of this our priority schedule is subject to revision from time to time. But generally speaking we have a good priority picture for our available labour.

National selective service-mobilization regulations provide:
that any employer may submit, at any time, for consideration by a mobilization board, a plan for the postponement of the military training of any group of its employees and a mobilization board may instruct any employer to submit such a plan if in its opinion such action is advisable.
Out of this provision we have developed not too recently an industrial mobilization survey plan. Basically the plan is to facilitate the orderly withdrawal of replaceable workers from essential industries into the armed services and to provide for their

replacement with the least possible disturbance to production. The survey requires the employer to report all employees, of military age, along with a description of the work they are doing and the length of time required to train replacements, particularly stressing the use of women.
The mobilization survey plan is reviewed by a local committee, located at each of the mobilization board centres. This committee is composed of a technically qualified chairman, familiar with modern production methods and a knowledge of the various skills and trades. Other members are, namely, a representative of the employment service, mobilization board, and the particular department of government involved. A plan, after passing through the committee is submitted to the mobilization board for approval; if approved it becomes an official schedule by means of which the employer is advised of the order in which his employees will be called.
Without going into details, I think the members will readily appreciate that any survey of this sort is also of utmost value to the employment service; first, to acquaint them of the employers' need for replacement; second, to inform them of any surplus labour.
It will be readily seen that the plan coordinates in a functional manner those agencies or departments of government most vitally concerned in a concerted effort.

There has been some instability in the general labour situation, but as I have said before it is a natural condition in war time and under the high pressure of war-time industrial operations. There are different situations arising requiring different conciliation approaches, and I am not one of those who feels that by a simple statement of labour policy the millennium will be reached. They have the Wagner act in the United States, a national labour relations board, a national war labour board, and still there are industrial disturbances in the country of our good friends to the south of us. There must foe more give and take on the part of employers and labour, a greater appreciation of the fairness of arbitration, and acceptance of the results of arbitration.
Recognition of the rights of labour to organize for collective negotiation of agreements is fundamental in a democracy such as ours. But we need more recognition of the responsibility which rests on both partners in industry.
It has been suggested in various quarters that the government has not made use of the experience and counsel of representatives of organized workers in matters touching Canada's war effort, particularly where the welfare of the workers is involved. I wish to refute this charge. I shall show that it has no foundation whatsoever in point of fact.
Connected with the Department of Labour, national selective service, the unemployment insurance commission and the national war labour board, are eight national councils, committees or boards, on all of which organized labour is represented. I might add that in and about the Department of Labour we have no boards or committees-except those which by their nature are restricted to our own officials-without labour representation.
I sometimes think, Mr. Chairman, particularly as regards national selective service on the employment side and on the conciliation side, that we have possibly taken too many men with stability and leadership out of the labour movement. I sometimes wonder whether it would not have been better to leave them where they were so that they could give the necessary leadership and stability that is required in an expanding industrial labour organization.
Does that apply from the minister down?

That may be true too, but I have always had a reputation for stability in my own community anyway, although I will say this to my hon. friend; it is not going to be said about me when this war is over that I sold the Canadian people down the river.
The eight national organizations to which I referred are: National Selective Service Advisory Board; Consultative Committees of the Ministry of Labour; National War Labour Board Committee; Advisory Council to Inter-departmental Committee on Labour-Management Production Committees; Vocational Training Advisory Committee; Unemployment Insurance Commission; Unemployment Insurance Advisory Committee; Unemployment Insurance National Employment Committee.
In addition to the national bodies which have labour representation, there are the nine regional war labour boards, the western labour board, and five regional employment advisory committees, on all of which labour is represented. Further there are some forty local employment advisory committees, all of them with labour representation, to advise in regard to employment matters; and there are thirty courts of referees under the Unemployment Insurance Act, to pass upon insurance claims which are questioned, and also to perform the important function of passing upon appeals taken under national selective service civilian regulations.

Most valuable assistance has been rendered by the national selective service advisory board. The board was established by order in council P.C. 2254 of March 21, 1942. It then consisted of the members of the interdepartmental committee on labour coordination and the members of the national war labour board.
The board was reconstituted by order in council P.C. 1788 of March 5, 1943, and now consists of five representatives nominated by organized labour, five representatives nominated by organized employers, one representative nominated by organized farmers, one representative of organized veterans, and a number of senior civil servants representing the departments which are most directly interested in problems of man-power, namely, Labour, Munitions and Supply, Agriculture, National Defence, Finance, and the Wartime Prices and Trade Board.
The board meets regularly on the second and fourth Wednesdays of every month and otherwise on special call.
The duties of the board are twofold: First, to bring to bear on all questions of man-power policy and on all major questions of manpower administration the points of view and advice of the interests or departments represented. Since its establishment, no significant regulation about man-power has been issued without prior discussion with, and approval by, the national selective service advisory board. Second, when its recommendations have been approved by the man-power committee of the cabinet and the governor general in council, to interpret and explain the policy thus approved to the interests or departments represented.
In other words, the national selective service advisory board is the major instrument for consultation and collaboration between government, organized employers, organized farmers and organized workers. I have been asked to explain how quotas are set for the call-up by military districts. The question itself is somewhat misleading since we are no longer operating on a district quota basis. The system is as follows: After the cabinet has authorized a given establishment the army requisitions the number of men required by military districts in accordance with the available facilities in its training centres. Those requisitions are transferred to the divisional registrars but are not regarded as quotas since their instructions are to call from within the designated age classes as many men as the machinery will permit.
Originally, since the army quotas were generally based on the population in the military

War Appropriation-Labour
age groups ini each district, the divisional registrars were given quotas based on population. Our present system, however, is to provide that all divisional registrars are calling at any given time from the same age classes. If, for example, the married men aged 19 to 25 are exhausted in one division sooner than in others, that division will not begin calling older married men until the other division has exhausted the younger age class.
On May 26 the hon. member for Lake Centre referred to what he considered an inequality in the percentage of the call-up for men for military service as between the different military districts. The fact that the percentage of enlistments and call-ups are both low in the same district or division would indicate that in such districts there is a higher percentage of men unfit for military service or that more men are required for farming and essential industry, or perhaps both. If the percentages of fit and unfit men were the same and the demands of farming and industry equal in each district or division, the district or division having a high percentage of volunteers would have a smaller percentage liable to the regulations and, consequently, a smaller percentage of men called up. The instructions to all mobilization divisions are to bring the men in the designated classes under the regulations as quickly as possible and to deal with them as rapidly as the machinery available permits. The districts vary in size. Some have greater difficulty in getting accommodation and staff. Therefore, the speed of selection varies, but, in the end, the result sought for is obtained- that is, all men fit for service, in the designated class, who are not given postponement and have not volunteered for service in the armed forces, are selected.
The hon. member for Lake Centre stated that there were some 91,800 Canadians, males, between the ages of 18-38 at present residing in the United States who have not given any indication that they will apply for United States citizenship and asked what was being done to secure the availability for service in the Canadian army of such men.
Canadians residing in the United States are subject to American mobilization regulations. They have the option of electing to serve in the Canadian forces. When a mobilization board has knowledge that a Canadian is residing in the United States the board does not proceed under the mobilization regulations. They are left for disposal by the American mobilization section.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury on the same day said that he had made inquiry as to
the basis of allocation of the quota for each military district and to his surprise had found that it was not on the available man-power but on the record of the voluntary enlistments in the district. That is not the case in so far as mobilization is concerned.

That was the case as stated by the Minister of National Defence for Air based on the theory of the number of non-permanent active militia units in the different military districts. That is where they got their volunteers and therefore it was on the basis of the volunteers that the call-up was made. I shall argue that question later.

In districts where there has been high voluntary enlistment the national defence training facilities would be taxed and the tendency might be to lower the allotment from such a district. That adds up to what my hon. friend has just said.
On the other hand it might happen that a district which supplied a very high number of volunteers in the past might have cleared its training centres and at present have more training facilities available, but these matters would not affect the number selected under mobilization. If there were not training facilities for men selected in their own districts they would be moved to a training centre where there was room.

I do not think that is fair. Speaking for myself, I was one who argued that we should do it that way, never thinking that it would land on my doorstep, but it did.	,

Our war emergency training programme, in cooperation with the provinces, has been of substantial assistance in relieving labour shortages, chiefly for semi-skilled jobs and meeting needs of the armed forces. As of March 31 last, nearly 218,248 men and women has been enrolled in the vocational and plant school classes since the beginning of the programme. In quoting that figure, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to hon. members that they look up the same kind of figures for the other united nations and they will find that, in a comparative sense, Canada's contribution redounds greatly to the credit of this country. This training programme has been most valuable to our war effort, and I believe that, as regards the work undertaken in these classes, we as Canadians can almost defy comparison. May I here pay tribute to our industrialists for the part played by them in these training classes which they carried on and which have permitted the erection of the gigantic industrial structure that we have built in the past four years. I would also, of course, express gratitude to the teachers in the schools, to the provincial governments and their officials, and to all those who have spent their time and labour unselfishly in this great cause.

organizations I have mentioned, also that provincial associations of professional engineers and other scientific and technical bodies. They have been most cooperative.
Through government financial aid to deserving students and promotion of summer employment of undergraduates in work which would contribute to their professional advancement we are preparing for future needs of technical personnel.

The government has sponsored short courses at our universities in personnel management. The objective is improved human relations in industry and as a natural sequence, improved production through more efficient use of labour.
As chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission when our industrial structure was expanding very rapidly, I personally saw the absolute need of the provision of personnel managers in many of the large industrial companies with which I came into contact. I think it is fair to say, while we have many brilliant engineers, the engineering of men is much more important and, may I say, much more difficult than the engineering of material things. I believe that the courses which have been carried on in our universities in cooperation with labour organizations and employers have been of tremendous assistance in building up this small army of personnel managers which will be of great benefit to our industrial structure not only at the moment but also in the days of peace which we hope are not very far away.
We have conducted job instructors' and job relations' courses and have been ready and willing to adopt any plan which would make our labour more skilled and thus more useful in the war effort.
That is our man-power achievements and programme. Criticize it if you like. But, and I appeal to you in all earnestness, please make your criticisms specific and practical. The problem is a national one, meriting the attention of all serious-minded citizens. Its solution demands the best effort that any of us can devote to it.
I would like to take this opportunity of recording my deep appreciation of the conscientious, efficient work of the staff of the Department of Labour.
With emergency conditions demanding emergency measures, new fegulations constantly being drafted, the staff of selective service and our employment service have had a real job to do. They have, in my opinion, done it well.	*
Too often we heed only the glamorous things; sometimes I envy the ministers of the fighting departments, but we must remember that there can be exceptional devotion to duty in the routine, more or less humdrum tasks of life. I also would like to extend my thanks to my colleagues of the government for constant cooperation. The man-power question is one affecting many departments of government. I have been strengthened by the understanding of my colleagues of the task assigned to me.

My first words, Mr. Chairman, must be of congratulation to the minister on the lengthy and complete statement he has made to-day in connection with the man-power situation. With regard to many of the matters of which he has spoken I am in complete agreement with him. In what he hadi to say during his peroration as to production, I know he spoke the views of all Canadians in that we are proud of Canada's record of achievement. However, I cannot agree with him when, in expressing his viewpoint in regard to the man-power situation in Canada, he used words to the effect that we have the best man-power policy that can be devised. In the use of those words, having regard to the conditions which have prevailed during-
My hon. friend is laughing, himself.

I have to laugh at that description. In regard to conditions prevailing in industry, shortages of man-power on the farms and the man-power situation in general the minister's opinion seemed to be that the steps taken were the best which could have been taken. That statement is a fine example of extravagance in overstatement. Great things have been done. The mobilization of Canada is something of which we are all proud. That is the attitude I have taken at all times, that when the government or the people of Canada are entitled to commendation, they should receive it.
The minister placed on record the numbers of men who are serving overseas to-day in the
various forces, and the number engaged in industry. To keep the record clear, it would be well to point out that at the time of the last war, with a population some forty-two per cent less than it is to-day, we enlisted 628,462 men for our armed forces, of whom 424,589 went overseas. As I listened to the minister to-day, I felt that in many respects he was apologetic for what he would like to carry into effect, namely, a system of selective service whereby men mobilized in Canada would be available for service at any point in the world. But that is denied to him because he and those associated with him have been shackled by considerations concerning which no further reference need be made.
The minister referred to a matter which I have raised on more than one occasion, namely, the need for equality of call and equality of administration of the National Resources Mobilization Act in every part of Canada. The answer he gave to-day does not meet the situation revealed by the records issued by the government. I am not going into detail in that connection, but I would1 refer the committee to Canada at War, in the February issue of which is set forth in detail the record of call-up in the various parts of Canada. I raised this matter in the house earlier in the session, and then indicated what the percentages were. I showed that under the call-up those provinces which were contributing the largest percentage of volunteers were also contributing the largest percentage of men called up for service in Canada under the measure of conscription in effect. The minister's answer to-day is not a denial of the accuracy of my statement, so far
War Appropriation*-Labour

as the percentages of call-up are concerned. London, Ontario, has a tremendous record for voluntary enlistments, and the call-up was 8-52 per cent of the available man-power; that of Kingston was 6'9 per cent; Halifax, 10-54 per cent, and Saint John, 9-89 per cent. On that earlier occasion I referred in detail to the various military districts, and I showed by figures which have not been contradicted that in other parts of Canada, where voluntary enlistments are a great deal lower than in the districts I have mentioned, the call-up was from forty per cent to fifty per cent less than in those districts in which voluntary enlistments were the most.
The minister says that is being corrected. Well, let us have the details. Interestingly enough, when this matter was discussed in the house, government statistics werfe available to the Canadian people, but since then, such information has been deleted from every issue of Canada at War. I ask again, as I asked the Minister of National Defence: Why was that deleted? I ask the minister in charge of the Department of Labour again to have that information restored in Canada at War in a form in which it will be readily available, so that there may be no misunderstanding as to whether or not the serious situation revealed therein that improper and unfair calls were being made has been terminated. If it has, then I will be the first to commend the government for having done so, just as I condemned the government before for having one system or rate of call in one part of Canada and another system of call in another part.
The minister stated to-day that recently a large number of changes have been made in the matter of compulsorily transferring men for service in various industries. I do not know what the record has been in the last few days, but I do know that up until June 6, 1943, only 9,000 men had been registered under the two orders then in effect. Those orders required that men working in various industries should register. I repeat that only 9,000 had registered, and of those registering, only ten per cent had been transferred. The minister claims that great work has been done by way of compulsorily transferring men to other branches of industry. I repeat that up to June 6 the record showed a total of ten per cent of 9,000.
When I asked the minister a perfectly fair question to-day, as to when the survey was made with respect to man-power, and whether the statements he was making were based upon a recent survey, his answer was that he would not permit any questions at that time. I suggest there is a perfectly good reason why the minister did not want to be asked the

question, because as late as May 4 only a very broad answer could be obtained. Into such an indifferent position had our man-power situation fallen that when the question was asked as to how many men the government expected to get through the registration of men engaged in the industries mentioned in the two orders in council, the reply was, "Unofficial estimates are that the number of men affected are somewhere between 10,000 and 50,000." Had there been any kind of survey up to that time, one would have expected an estimate somewhat close to the facts and the results.
It indicates clearly that up to May 4, 1943, there had been no survey of man-power in Canada. On more than one occasion I, along with other hon. members on this side of the house, have asked the government to let the country know what has been done in connection with the registration of man-power, how many men are available for the armed services, and how many men will be available for industry and agriculture. This is the fourth year of the war, and yet there is no plan today for Canada, in so far as allocation of man-power is concerned.
As a matter of fact if hon. members want to get information in regard to the labour situation, the^ have to go outside the house to get it from officials of the department who make speeches elsewhere than in the House of Commons, and, in the case I have in mind, elsewhere than in Canada. I was in the library yesterday, and I picked up the May, 1943, issue of the proceedings of the academy of political science. A meeting of this organization was held in New York on April 7, 1943, and among those who spoke was the director of national selective service of Canada. Mr. MacNamara dealt with the man-power situation and explained why it was impossible to do many of the things the government would like to do. He set out in detail the policy of the government. My hon. friends on the government side never admit that they have brought in conscription; they do not admit that the present system is a means by which men are forced to volunteer in the armed forces for overseas service, but when the deputy minister of labour was speaking at this meeting he endeavoured to explain to those who were present why it was that Canada did not have selective service by w'hich men would serve all over the world just as they have in the United States. He said:
Canada's armed forces consist primarily of volunteers, but the method of voluntary recruiting is supplemented by conscription for service in Canada.

Since a very large proportion of the draftees enlist for active service anywhere, either before or after their induction into the service, the net effect of our draft is not very different from yours.
At last we have from the mouth of an official of the Department of Labour definite proof of what we have been endeavouring to place before the house on more than one occasion, that Canada has conscription. Apparently he wanted to show that Canada had a plan. He said that from the end of 1940 down into 1941:
Employers often tried to recruit and train young workers, only to find after a few months that they would be called or would volunteer for the armed services. All of us had our sights set too low. Most employers at this stage, for example, refused to believe that they would ever find it necessary to replace men by women. But Canada's war effort continued to expand without any serious dislocation of other activities by the natural and almost automatic turnover of labour in search of better jobs.
The minister, along with his predecessors, took pride in the man-power plan of the government. We heard that pride expressed in 1940; we heard the' same statement made in 1941 and again in 1942. What does this gentleman say? He said:
There was no central authority directing the movement, no master plan, although conscription and training for war industry had begun.
Referring to the fact that man-power had been lost to agriculture and indicating that there was no plan, he said:
The steady drain of agricultural man-power to the forces and the war industries has thus been checked.
And again, farther along in his speech, he said:
Our present plans through March 31 of next year call for a net increase of over 160,000 men for the armed services, agriculture and war production.
Why is it that we could not be told in this house that 160,000 men are to be required next year when the man who administers this department gives to a gathering in the United States information which has been denied to parliament? I pass on to another statement which was made, as follows:
At the other end, in the less essential occupations, not only will men be called for military service in the regular routine, but substantial numbers of those found unfit or who have previously been found unfit will have to be released by their employers and required to take available' essential work. If this proves to be in agriculture, as we expect in many cases, the difficulty arising from the fact that agricultural wages are so much lower than industrial wages will be met by pointing out that each such man will earn at least as much as in the army.
The whole plan regarding man-power which has been denied to parliament is placed before the academy of political science. I would ask the minister to elucidate this next statement which I am going to quote, because parliament has not yet had this information. He said:
I have ignored many of the details of our regulations-the inevitable exceptions, the provision of travelling expenses, separation allowances and other special allowances to encourage workers to accept distant jobs-
Are separation allowances being paid to-day to men transferred from one industry to another? Are separation allowances being paid to their families? I continue:
-the right given to workers who are transferred to more essential jobs to claim reinstatement without loss of seniority in their old jobs when the more essential work is finished.
Have such regulations been brought into effect? They have certainly not yet been brought before parliament.
I must get on with some other matters to which I wish to refer. All of this indicates that in spite of the fact that emergency regulations have been issued by the department from time to time since March, 1942, we are still in the same position we always were in so far as compulsion is concerned, except with respect to the two groups of occupations referred to in the orders in council issued in May last. Fifteen months ago the Prime Minister declared for a policy of the negative compulsion of restriction. Time has shown that the policy that has been carried into effect has been a positive restriction of compulsion except in so far as it is necessary to force men to volunteer for overseas service instead of adopting selective service. Unless a true form of selective service is brought in, neither the minister nor any department of government will have the power or the support of the people of Canada to move men back and forth from one industry to another regardless of their personal wishes.
All of this was predicted last fall by Mr. Elliott Little when he said that there would still be a few months' grace before the situation became unmanageable. That is how it has worked out. To-day we find ourselves in the position where man-power is not available, not through the shortage of man-power-this was made quite clear some months ago by Doctor Couper of the Department of Labour -but because there is a shortage of the right men in the right place at the right time owing to the failure of the government to adopt a practical policy. Mr. Little recommended many things which were ridiculed at the time, of which some have since been adopted. The

events that have occurred since he resigned have entirely justified everything he said at the time. In part he said this:
It might be well to point out that the prospects for the winter are for a continuation of the present situation; that is, for a fairly tight general condition, with some particularly acute local and industrial problems, but not reaching an overall shortage of really critical proportions until spring.
In the same memorandum Mr. Little also pointed out:
Some of the special difficulties which already exist, such as the all-around shortage of ablebodied men, qualified for heavy and relatively low-paid work in the base metal and coal mines, smelters, foundries and steel mills, in branches of the lumbering and agricultural industries, will have cumulatively more serious effects on essential production.
What he said then has come true; what he warned of then has culminated in a situation that is now prevalent in all parts of Canada. Our mines are undermanned, it is admitted now; our farms have been depleted of man-power, so that men shall serve for the defence of Canada but not beyond the confines of Canada. The minister claims that the record to date of man-power on the farms has been a creditable one. But the minister could not assert in the agricultural portions of this country that the policy he enunciated to-day has been carried into effect since March, 1942. The promise was made then that essential man-power on the farms would receive postponement unless the boards were able to establish non-essentiality on the part of the farm worker. The regulations were there, but regulations without enforcement are words without works.
Boards were set up. But those boards did not carry out the regulations. The minister to-day endeavours to put the responsibility on the boards. The responsibility rests upon the government for failure to set up machinery to carry into effect the policy enunciated by the government. All over the dominion the situation has been such that in one province there has been strict adherence to the regulations, while in another province there has been a failure to observe the regulations. That is the reason why two years ago I made a suggestion which I thought would be of assistance. It was that there should be a court of appeal, consisting of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada not to hear every appeal that would come before it in the ordinary way, but to hear only appeals from persons who believed that the interpretation of the regulations with respect to them was not according to the law of the land, and those persons should only then have a right of
appeal after leave had been granted. If that had been done, there would have been equality of call, and certainly equality of administration.
To-day the coal mining industry is depleted of its man-power, all because there has been no selective service. True, this is selective service in name but not in practice. It is not in effect.
The minister says that the people of Canada as a whole are satisfied with the man-power policy of this government. Let me refer him to what has been said on that point by an outstanding Canadian, the president of the Canadian Legion, who, on June 7, speaking in Edmonton, said:
Apart from certain compulsory man-power measures recently introduced on the home front, we seem to be as far away as ever from a realistic policy of total war and I'm afraid that both our government and people are in for a rude awakening when our army casualties start to come in in earnest.
The problem of man-power is a question no country at war can afford to pussyfoot about, and we know that when the great test comes, it is man-power more than anything else that will tip the scales of victory or defeat.
Are we getting that man-power to-day? Brigadier James Mess, deputy adjutant-general and director of army recruiting, speaking in Toronto on June 18, said:
Every man and woman medically fit is needed in the fighting services. It's just as important to get a girl in the services as it is to get a man. Those in industry may disagree hut every girl or man they lose is no tragedy to them-[DOT] it's an inconvenience.
A process has been going on for four years whereby man-power is subject to the attraction of the armed forces, the attraction of industry or the call of agriculture. The result has been that various ministers have been compelled to admit during the course of the man-power debate that the services under their control are short of the necessary manpower, each minister being in the position of a residuary legatee and receiving only what is left over after the conflicting claims of either armed forces or industry or agriculture have been met.
We are not getting the men. Requisitions for men are made by the defence department. The story is told in the latest return that was brought down on June 17, 1943. Requisitions were sent out for 104,684 men for the army between October 31 and June 17; and how many were secured? The number that answered the call was 52,459, or only forty-three per cent of the number required, and they must have been required or the calls would not have been sent out. Deduct from

May I now summarize to the committee the points of view which I had been making before the recess. We of the opposition demand in the interests of Canadian unity and of an all-out war effort, first, that there be one equality of service everywhere in Canada, and, second, that under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act there shall be equality in enrolment and in the administration of the act. I am not going into details with regard to the statement I am about to make, but I have spent a considerable amount of time analysing the figures of the call-up in the various provinces, and I say without fear of contradiction that had there been equality of call in every province in Canada, up until December 1, 1942, there would be no shortage of man-power on the farms of western Canada and the province of Ontario, where I know there are shortages now. The minister has stated that from now on there are to be calls made in the country as a whole. Against that I protest, for in doing that all opportunity of securing equality of call will be denied, and there will be no way in which there can be a check-up to ascertain whether or not the law is being equally applied and enforced.
We demand that there shall be equality of enforcement. The minister produced a lot of figures to-day in a statement of the national selective service on man-power, which I believe he said was being placed on Hansard. That statement, even from a casual perusal, is a kind of mathematical sleight-of-hand. The figures that are given do not, I submit, give the picture as it is.
In connection with the enforcement of the law, a return was brought down on January 29, 1943, in regard to the penalties that had been imposed for infractions of the law throughout Canada. Hon. members will notice that in division A there is only one prosecution, and in division B the penalties run generally from three to six months. In division D penalties consist of one fine of $25 and costs, and sentences of six months and two years in penitentiary. In division E, with the exception of one or two gaol sentences, the penalty for failure to report for military training consists of fines of from $1 and costs to $50, $25 and costs, $5 and costs, costs plus $20 and the like, and the same applies to division F. In other districts you will find the penalties imposed for failure to report are generally gaol sentences.
If there is to be any enforcement of the law there must be such enforcement that, when infractions are ascertained and guilt established, the enforcement will not be so small as to result in penalizing the man who carries out the law. Some of the penalties that have been imposed are unfair and unequal, having regard tfo penalties being imposed in other parts of the country. I say that in certain districts the man who is a defaulter and does not answer the call is actually the better for not having done so. He can earn the wages available to him outside the army, realizing that when he is brought before the court the penalty will be so low as not to amount to a detriment. This unequal enforcement of the regulations in respect of call-up has resulted in a total absurdity from the point of view of the administration of justice in Canada.
The figures that were given in February, while Canada was at war, are figures of the department of information. I repeat what I said on a previous occasion, that, having regard to the statistics given therein, there are to-day in Canada, unaccounted for, or there were in February last, 205,776 men. I put the figures on Hansard earlier in the session. Has there been any enforcement since? Yes, there has been enforcement to the extent of a very few prosecutions, the total number being 1,326. There has also been a promise of immunity,

whereby in return for reporting there was to be no prosecution, and the total number that answered the call on the strength of immunity is approximately 7,200.
These statistics, which cannot be denied, show that no serious endeavour has been made to enforce the law. Now then, Mr. Chairman, I put this to you. When there is a law on the statute books which takes from a man the liberty he enjoys of going where he pleases and doing what he pleases in general, and places him in the armed service, and that law is not equally enforced, or at any rate not seriously enforced, the whole administration of justice is brought into disrepute.
Why are not the mounted police used in locating defaulters? Recently the government appointed an institution in Toronto, a credit bureau. It went to work on the matter. I had the figures before me a moment ago, but I cannot put my hand on them just now, but they show that there were located in Toronto or the province of Ontario fewer than 300; and none elsewhere.
Three hundred and fifty approximately.

What a record of enforcement, having regard to the number I have given of 205,000! I do not think my hon, friend is serious when he says that.

I tried to ask some questions of the minister, and he said he did not want to be interrupted. I am serious when I say that there has been no answer from the minister to the statement which I have made on several occasions, that there is not now, nor has there been, any endeavour-

In that connection, the minister to-day placed on the record a plan showing the manpower of this dominion employed in industry and agriculture. As late as last January-to be exact on January 14, 1943*-the answer which was given, when the question was asked by the hon. member for Rosedale as to the number of persons engaged in manufacturing industries, was that the information was not available, and would not 'be until the tabulation of the April returns of the unemployment insurance commission; and with regard to agriculture, the answer was given that the last figures the government had were of the census of June 1, 1941.
I commend the minister for having utilized the services of the unemployment insurance and other bodies throughout Canada to secure an up-to-the-minute census showing how many men and women are employed in the various industries, for it is only with such a picture that anyone can arrive at a proper conclusion as to whether or not there is a proper allocation and use of man-power which there should be. I may add that even now there is no control of man-power in Canada under selective service to prevent men from moving backwards and forwards within the same industry or even outside the same industry.
On Monday, June 21, the Minister of Munitions and Supply referred to the changing personnel in the shipbuilding industry. I asked him, as reported in Hansard at page 3839:
I want to know if men are still being called up from these specialized jobs-
