According to this
representative on the national coal committee, the government brought him here to face a decision already made without consultation.

Mr. Chairman, the committee listened attentively to the statement of the minister this afternoon. It was rather long and evidently, if we are to judge by the criticism of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, it was not satisfactory. I think the position this group has taken in regard to labour matters is that we are not concerned so much with the mechanics of organization, but rather with what we consider the wrong attitude adopted by the government in regard to labour's part in our war effort. I wish to be quite fair with the minister, so that I am going to state at once that he has had a very difficult task with which to deal. If there is lack of organization; if there is confusion and misunderstanding in the Department of Labour-and I believe everj'one agrees there is-I think we can absolve the minister of at least some of the blame, though he must assume a certain responsibility and must be prepared to accept or to listen to criticism in connection with that share of it.
Labour-industrial relations as they exist in Canada at the present time roots from the attitude of the government and1 the business men of this country who have had so much to do with the organization of industry since the beginning of the war. That being so, the government as a whole must accept the major responsibility. The attitude of the government was first indicated very early in the war, when it became clear that they did not realize the importance of labour in the war effort . Let me remind hon. members of what happened. When the war broke out, one of the most efficient and most imaginative ministers in the cabinet, the late Hon. Norman Rogers, was transferred from his position as Minister of Labour to the position of Minister of National Defence. I am not finding fault with the government for shifting a capable minister to

what it might consider a more responsible department, but it indicates a failure on the part of the government to understand the importance of labour in the issues that were confronting the country. The change in the Department of Labour might not have resulted in any great difficulty if the government had appointed a minister who had some understanding of labour matters. Instead of appointing such a man, they appointed a wealthy lawyer. I have no objection to lawyers as a class, though I am inclined to believe that in a cooperative society they would not have any place, because where some one would not be seeking to cheat someone else, there would be nothing for them to do. My point, however, is that right at the beginning, when we ought to have made the best possible start, we appointed as head of the labour department a man who knew very little about labour and who had no associations with the organized labour movement.
So that from the very beginning the workers have not been considered as human beings or as members of the community entitled to a voice in determining the conditions under which they would work. Not only have they not been considered entitled to a voice in determining, working conditions; they have not been permitted to have a voice in determining direction of policy. The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the matter of labour representation on war boards. The Minister of Labour says that labour is represented. I have stated1 previously in this house that to the extent that labour was represented on any board, it was merely a token representation, and it was never intended that labour should be consulted. I think the proof of that statement is to be found in the fact that when the first order in council was passed freezing wages, the national labour council, which was then in existence, was not even consulted, though the order in council materially affected the conditions of labour.

I know my hon. friend does not want to convey a wrong impression, but I was secretary of the national labour supply council at that time, and I have a vivid recollection of the consultations that took place with respect to the provisions of the order in council stabilizing wages. I am not suggesting that the opinion was unanimous.

I have placed these facts on record previously. I have not the facts before me at the moment, but it was quite clear that labour was not consulted in that instance. As a matter of fact I do not think labour knew anything about the matter until the Prime Minister made his radio address announcing the policy.

War Appropriation-Labour

The hon. member was
talking about the labour supply council, and that is what I am referring to. I do not say a general convention was held. If I remember correctly, there were at that time on the labour supply council Tom Moore, Mr. Mosher, Jack Bruce and, I think, Howard Chase, though I may be mistaken, and they were consulted. I am not going to say that they agreed with the government policy, but they were consulted.

Well, we will not argue the point; I shall bring the evidence here again. I suggest to the minister that he was insistent he should not be interrupted during the course of his speech, so that he might allow me to carry on with what may be distasteful to him, since I allowed him to carry on with what was distasteful to me.
Very well; I am sorry.

Of course to anyone who
has had anything to do with the labour movement in this country that attitude is quite understandable. Neither the government nor business in this country has got away from the old-fashioned idea that labour is a commodity, that its price can be regulated by the law of supply and demand. They may think it is unfortunate that the individual, in which labour power or the labour commodity is embodied, has to. go around to deliver it. So far as they are concerned the individual workman is merely the wrapper in which the commodity is contained. Until we get away from that point of view and consider the workers as human beings, as members of the community, as people who are interested in all the affairs of our society and who should be consulted at every turn, conditions will not improve. I say that because to-day workers are the most important people in society.
Instead, then, of appointing a lawyer to the Department of Labour, the government should have endeavoured to get someone as head of that department who would feel about it, and the factors with which he had to deal, in much the same way as the Minister of Finance feels about financial matters, the Minister of Munitions and Supply about the organization of production, or the Minister of National Defence about military affairs. If we had something like that, there would be someone in the department who would stand up for labour, and I am satisfied we would not be in the difficulties we are in to-day.
Instead of that, however, the Department of Labour was a sort of Cinderella among
government departments, and to-day we are paying for that view. The Department of Labour and the minister are paying the price in inefficient organization. The other departments took the cream of the executive staff available before the* needs of the Department of Labour were realized. I am satisfied that in no department of government is it more important to have a specially trained personnel than in the Department of Labour. That department, more than any other, deals with the human factor in the war effort.
This afternoon the minister took up most of his time in dealing with the government's man-power policy. There are two aspects of the problem, namely the policy itself, and the administration of that policy. As I said before, the government as a whole must accept the responsibility for the policy, and at the most the Minister of Labour can be held responsible only for its administration. I consider that from the beginning of the war our labour policies have been wrong on account of our attitude toward labour. They have been wrong in another way. We have never come to a decision as to what portion of the labour force in Canada should go into the armed forces, and what portion should be available for production.
It is true that man-power policy cannot be static. It changes with developments in the military situation. I am convinced that at the present time the emphasis on man-power in Canada should be placed on production, rather than on men for the armed forces. Speaking in the house a week ago, the Minister of Munitions and Supply pointed out that only one-third of Canada's war production is for our own military forces. Consequently two-thirds of our production goes to the other united nations. I believe the Minister of Munitions and Supply put the case for what I am now saying when he spoke last year in one of the debates. I find these words at page 3371 of Hansard of June 16, 1942:
In deciding our man-power policy we must consider whether we can contribute more to victory by continuing to be a principal source of munitions and supplies for the united nations, or whether we can make our greatest contribution by limiting our production in order to send overseas every physically fit man. ... It seems to me that our whole ivar effort is being distorted at the present time by the undue emphasis now being placed on men for the army overseas.
Then he continued:
I base my view's on the fact that the supply of man-power for the armed services and for war production is not unlimited.
Canada is not the only country which finds itself in a position where demands for manpower may have to be met even by shifting
War Appropriation-Labour

men from the armed forces. I hold in my hand the Commercial Intelligence Journal of June 12, 1943, in which is a report on conditions in New Zealand. It is credited to Mr. C. B. Birkett, Canada's acting trade commissioner in that country. He points out that in New Zealand they have come to the conclusion that they have put too many men into the armed forces, and that it may now be necessary to take men from the armed forces into production, if production is to be kept up. After pointing out what' New Zealand has done in connection with supplying men for the armed forces, he says:
While this effort has been a splendid one, the opinion is generally held that New Zealand is over-committed in regard to the supply of men for the forces to the extent of seriously endangering production levels and the maintenance of public utilities. Much hardship has been experienced in the past year from the reduction of office and factory staffs, and of available farm labour. The loss of man-power to the railways, postal services and electric power schemes, despite the employment of women, has been particularly serious. Efforts to remedy the situation without interfering with established programmes, such as a transfer of over 6,000 men from non-essential to essential work and a return of between 8,000 and 10,000 men from the army to work on the farms, have proved inadequate.
I think we may have to change our minds in the matter of man-power in the interest of our war effort. That is, if our armed forces and our production are to be used to the greatest advantage in the global war in which we are engaged. We are all agreed that production in Canada has been large in comparison with the population of the country. We are a considerable distance from the theatres of war, and there are millions of men in the united nations who are ready to fight if they are given the arms, equipment and food necessary to carry on. If Canada can make a better effort by supplying these things, I think it would be the part of wisdom for this government and this parliament to direct our efforts in that direction.
For a few minutes I should like to refer to employer-employee management committees. On April 15 a return was made, I think in response to a motion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, giving the number of plants in Canada in which there were production committees. The return states that the number of firms having established committees is 851, and the total number of employees of such firms is 486,896. I do not know what means the department had at their disposal to get this information, but after questioning employees of some of the firms whose names appear on this list I am doubtful if there are

management production committees in many of the plants mentioned. I have information from Massey-Harris, Toronto, that there is a production committee in name only. The de Havilland aircraft, Toronto-tentative agreement between company and union to establish committee; still negotiating agreement, but no committee established. Wilson Motor Bodies Limited, Long Branch - discussions taking place, but no committee. Clarke Ruse Aircraft, Nova Scotia-no committee. Chrysler Corporation, Windsor - exploring situation; no committee as yet.
I could give a list of more than a dozen firms, the employees of which gave the same answer-no committee. I am doubtful if there are many real employer-employee committees in Canada. The reason for this is that Canadian employers are opposed to that sort of labour-employer cooperation. There is no doubt that these committees are extremely helpful in improving production. I have in my hand " Labour News from Great Britain," which contains an article by Herbert Tracey of the British trades union congress. He has this to say in reference to employer-employee committees:
As an important aid towards this organization of production, the congress-
That is the British trades union congress.
-welcomed the development of joint workshop and other production committees, and urged that these should be increasingly recognized as an effective means of promoting the maximum output of goods and " services, material and equipment.
At the same time the Scottish congress pointed out that the necessity for maximum effort must not be regarded as applying only to those undertakings directly producing arms and war materials. Industries and services are so interrelated with the war effort that they must all be made to run smoothly if the military and social security of the nation is to be adequately safeguarded.
I note that when Elliott Little became director of national selective service he was anxious that committees of this kind should be established. Probably that is one of the reasons why he could not get along in the Department of Labour. In an address to the Quebec section of the Canadian weekly newspapers' association, held in Toronto on Saturday, May 9, 1942, shortly after he began his work, he had something to say about the opposition of employers to cooperating with labour. He said:
I'll tell you quite frankly that we have been given information about some employers deliberately stimulating the movement of labour to and from their plants with the definite purpose of persuading the government that it was necessary to freeze all labour to present jobs. I have had employers try to sell me on a policy

War Appropriation-Labour
of blanket freezing. In their view, there were advantages-but only until I pointed out that freezing worked two ways: that if you froze labour you not only took the right to quit away from the worker, but the right to fire away from the employer. When they thought about it that way, their enthusiasm for a freezing order disappeared.
I think it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South who mentioned in the house the other evening that in nearly every strike that had taken place in this country since the war began, the workers had not gone deliberately on strike. In nearly every stoppage of work they had been manoeuvred into such action by means of tactics such as were referred to by Mr. Little in that speech. Having referred to the ways and means of organizing production, he said:
Do not mistake what I am talking about. By better employer-employee relations I do not mean a concession to the workers here, a privilege there, such as a cup of tea at four o'clock. Those things have their place. I am talking about the whole broad field of personnel management which boils down to mean the best possible personal relations between management and the employees. The workers I meet and have worked with do not want employers to hold their hand. They simply asked to be treated as you want to be treated-as an adult and a responsible citizen.
That is the very thing the government has been loath to do; it is the very thing that employers have refused to do.
Continuing, Mr. Little said:
Better employer-employee relations can produce more tanks, planes, and guns; they will help sell war savings certificates, they will put over the victory bond drives. Secured now out of this struggle for our lives, it should be obvious to the dullest mind that they can be made the foundation of our industrial and social reconstruction in the post-war period.
The people that Elliott Little had to deal with were not people who could see as far as the post-war period. They could see only as far as the interests of their own immediate industry were concerned, and they were very much afraid that if they had to cooperate with labour during the war, it would mean that they would have to cooperate with labour after the war, and that is the last thing they hope will come out of the war.
The minister quoted from Ernest Bevin this afternoon. May I make a brief quotation from a speech by Ernest Bevin, which can be found on page 127 of the collection of his speeches entitled "The Balance Sheet of the Future"? Mr. Bevin states there:
This task of winning the war means you have to call for the utmost ingenuity you can get from the people, for every ounce of ability they have, for the willingness and courage to take decisions, to make them indifferent to enemy action and carry on. I do not believe you can do that with orders from the top.
Every attempt to get anything out of the workers in Canada since the war began has been made by orders from the top.
The minister this afternoon devoted very little time to the matter of labour organization and the difficulty that labour has to get recognition from employers in industry. The only reference he made to that subject was, I think, that the right of labour to organize is fundamental. If the right of labour to organize is fundamental-

I was dealing there with selective service, which is mentioned in the estimates. I thought management and labour could be dealt with in the discussion of my estimates in supply. I just wanted to make that clear.

That is all right. But it is nevertheless an exceedingly important matter. May I ask again, if the right of labour to organize is fundamental, and if that right is recognized by the government as fundamental, what is it that is preventing labour organization? I asked the minister the other day about the lay-off of men at the Rand-Ingersoll company plant at Sherbrooke.' In replying to the question the minister said there was a report that the men had been laid off-note this-on account of trade union activities. These men are engaged in war work. I believe that they are producing engines or the material for engines for our cargo ships or it may be naval vessels. Whatever may have been the reason why these men were laid off, the fact of the matter is that the lay-off did not begin until the men began to organize, and the lay-off took place only in those parts of the plant where the men were organized. Ever since the war began, it has been the same story in almost all of Canada's war industries. In every one of them where to-day there is recognition for labour, that recognition has been attained only after a struggle and often by the threat of a strike. I have before me the submission of the Montreal Aircraft Lodge, 712, of the International Association of Machinists, to the national war labour board inquiry, and I think it would be interesting to read just one short paragraph, which is illustrative. When I read it the committee will have a picture of every submission made by every labour organization which appeared before the national war labour board. This is what it says:
We set about organizing the plant, and then asked the company to negotiate an agreement with our organization, similar to that in force in our other plants. This the company refused to do, and on September 26, 1941, we applied for a hoard of conciliation. At that time, practically 100 per cent of the employees in this plant "were members in good standing of our
War Appropriation-Labour

organization. On one pretext or another, under the guise of attempts by the Department of Labour to "conciliate" the dispute, the board was not established until May, 1942.
Remember, the application for a board was made in September, 1941, and the board was only granted in May, 1942. The submission continues:
In the interval, the company had used every trick, including intimidation, mass lay-offs, and the use of the company-union set-up which existed in the car-building section of the works, to destroy the organization. When we complained recently in a letter to the Prime Minister of the dilatoriness of the department in establishing this board of conciliation, the minister defended himself by stating that our organization had agreed to the delay in that we had concurred with and participated in the conciliation efforts of his department. We can only conclude that the minister took our failure to go on strike illegally during this period as a sign of agreement with the delay, because we used every other form of representation known to us to constantly urge the speedy settlement of this matter, and complained many times of the delay.
Could anything more clearly illustrate that if the right to organize is a fundamental right, the workers in Canada are denied that fundamental right?
Earlier in the session, when I spoke in this house on some other matter, I pointed out that the government took the same attitude in those industries under its own control, and that it was not until December, 1942, more than three years after the war began, that the right of labour to organize was accepted in these crown companies.
I see my time is about up, and I will conclude with this. In the submission made to the war labour board by Mr. A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian congress of labour, he makes this statement in reference to order in council P.C. 2685, which declared the fundamental right to organize:
It was also ignored by the government itself, as organized employees of crown companies were not permitted to negotiate with the managements or these companies although they were under the direct control of the government. However, after strikes had been threatened in several crown companies, order in council P.C. 10802 was passed in December, 1942, permitting the employees to join unions and permitting the managements to negotiate collective agreements. In spite of the recommendations made by tlie congress to the government the order does not yet apply to the^ Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or the National Harbours Board.
_ I would suggest to the minister that if the right to organize is a fundamental right, he as Minister of Labour has the bounden duty to see that labour is protected in the exercising of that fundamental right.

I listened with a good deal of interest to the minister's statement this afternoon and in commenting upon it now I have no wish to traverse the universe. I shall direct my attention to one particular subject about which the minister did not say a great deal. I notice, in the little programme that has been given to us in order that we may pursue an orderly discussion, that there are about twenty-two items constituting an expenditure of about 821,500,000. I am quite certain that when we get through with these twenty-two items we shall have pretty well exhausted the administration of the Department of Labour.
The item which I wish to discuss does not seem to appear anywhere on this programme. About a month ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) issued what was known as a statement recognizing that a national emergency existed in connection with the fuel supplies of Canada. About a couple of weeks ago, on the orders of the day, I asked whether the Minister of Labour would care to make a statement informing the country what progress was being made with respect to this national emergency. He rose and made some little statement that did not amount to anything, and I suggested to him. that if he could not make a statement, then it would be all right for him to do so in a few days' time. A couple of weeks have now gone by, and when he made his speech this afternoon he seemed to have forgotten somehow or another that this national emergency existed, because it is the only national emergency we have, or the only one that has been announced apart from the obvious emergency of the war, and yet he made only a passing reference to it.
I shall have something to say with reference to the announcement of that national emergency. If we think deeply enough into this whole matter of the national emergency on account of the fuel, supply we shall recognize, I believe, that the only reason why there is such an emergency in Canada is that the present Liberal administration of Canada were unable to see far enough ahead, or else they closed their eyes to that which was very obvious. In respect of the announcement of a national coal emergency, I think it would have been proper to announce that there was a great Liberal administration emergency. I suggest that judgment should begin at home, where it belongs, and it would have been fitting for the Prime Minister of Canada to announce this and to say: We did not foresee this, or our expert advisers did not tell us this would happen, and now, by reason of

War Appropriation-Labour
our lack of foresight, I have to announce a national emergency on account of the shortage of fuel.
I had something to say about this last night when I asked the Minister of Munitions and Supply a question or two, in reply to which he said that he recognized' the seriousness of the present fuel situation in Canada. I have reason to believe that the situation is serious, and I believe that the people of Canada should be told immediately and should foe given a comprehensive picture to show, exactly how the situation stands to-day.
As I see it, the supply of coal falls very heavily upon, shall I say, three categories. We must supply our armed forces with the fuel, the coal, they need. This includes not only the army camps and so forth, but the fuelling of ships. I think the minister should tell us something about that. He rose a little while ago, interrupting a previous speaker, and asked: Does my hon. friend know that we are building more merchant ships in Canada to-day than ever before, even more than Great Britain? That being the case, might I also add that these merchant ships need coal. Are they going to get it? I wonder what it would mean if this country should suddenly realize that ships cannot sail from our harbours because they have no coal.
Did the hon. member ever hear of oil burners?
Who piped up then?
I asked if you ever heard of oil burners.
I cannot hear what the hon. member is trying to say. Oh, well, it is all right; I imagine it was not anything very important he asked me anyway.

You would not be able to
answer it anyway.
It was about oil burners.

I asked the minister about that, and he said that some of the ships were fuelling with oil but that many were fuelling with coal. Perhaps there is an oil emergency too. Does my hon. friend recognize that? Does my hon. friend recognize that Canada has oil, but that it is under the ground and that our administration in years gone by have so lacked foresight that they have not been able to get it out of the ground? Does my hon. friend know that? Not only must coal be supplied to our armed forces, but it must be available to our industries, or the consequences will be serious. The third category is the domestic consumer.
Are the people of Canada to be cold this winter? These are three things the minister should tell Canada: is he going to guarantee that our armed forces, our industrial areas, and our domestic consumers will be supplied?
In respect of man-power in coal mines, I know' of course that the minister appreciates there is difficulty in that regard. But that difficulty would not have arisen if the present administration had taken a long-range view of a proper and adequate national man-power policy. When war broke out, coal miners volunteered for the services. Many of them did so because they could not get full-time employment in the mines; they said, "We will enlist, we can make more money; at least, our families will be cared for. The coal mining industry is too uncertain; it is a hit-or-miss proposition". Accordingly many of our coal miners volunteered. I wonder whether the minister can tell us how many coal miners are in the armed forces, and how many are overseas. I do not believe he can. I challenge him to tell us.
Can you?
No. I am not administering this country.
Another straw man.
We had a national registration some years ago. Men had to report their employment, their trade.
That was to find out how they would vote.

I do not know whether, when a man joins the army, he states what his civilian occupation is. But if the federal administration is what I think it should be, it should know exactly how many men of the different trades there are in the armed forces, and where they are.
So much for that. Not only did many coal miners volunteer for the armed forces, but many of them went into other kinds of work because they could get more pay there. I know that a great many Crowsnest pass miners moved out to Vancouver or some other coast city and engaged in shipbuilding work. It may have been an admirable thing to do, I do not know; but at the present time we are short of coal miners, and I do not know whether the government intend to urge these coal miners to return to their work. Perhaps they will. What we are now facing is an emergency, and there is compulsion with respect to the moving of men from one industry to another. But if coal miners who left
War Appropriation-Labour

their jobs, sold their homes, pulled up stakes and moved to another part of the country, as I know some of them did, are now to be recalled to go into coal mining, it is only fair that the government should compensate them for loss on the sale of their homes and whatever other expense may have been involved, to the extent of every cent of loss. Another thing the government should do is to assure these miners that when they return they will have proper employment, not only for the duration of the war but after the war. I know that some will say, " How do we know that we shall be able to get markets for our coal after the war?" Well, the greatest market for Canadian coal is right here in Canada, and if this country had a proper national coal policy, every mine in the country could be running at full capacity and employing its full number of miners during peace time.
Another factor which might cause some shortage or accentuate the present national emergency in respect of the production of coal is that much of our coal has been coming from the United States, which is now experiencing serious labour difficulties. What the Americans do is their own business; I shall not say anything about that. But comparatively speaking, Canada has been fortunate in that there has not been more trouble in the coal mining industry of Canada. I am not going to give the Department of Labour or the government any credit for that.
We would not expect you to.

I believe that any credit that is due is coming to our own coal miners. There have been one or two small local upsets, but no general disruption of the industry has occurred, and I believe the coal miners are to be complimented upon the fact.
There is a tremendous man-power problem in respect of this industry, but I am not going to blame the minister for that. It dates from a long way further back than the minister's connection with the Department of Labour. He inherited the situation; it is a baby which was left on his doorstep.
And he is not a very good papa.

He may not be a very good papa. As a matter of fact it was not a very nice baby they left there for him to handle. I am, therefore, not going to blame him so much. It has been said that there has been a sort of bungling man-power policy. I know the minister does not like that term; he has evidenced his dislike of it before. I am not saying that he has bungled; I am saying

it dates a long way back and has its root cause in the fact that the government has been lacking in foresight with respect to the manpower policy of this country ever since the war began.
What was the situation before the war started? The coal mines of this country were operating on part time; men were on relief, and we could not dispose of our coal. Of course we realize that we did not need as much coal then as we need now, but we know also that the United States coal combines held a good share of the Canadian market. Even in those days if there had been a proper national fuel policy, the coal mines of Canada could have been operating at full capacity, and there would have been no need for coal miners to leave their jobs and go into other branches of war industry. But, you see, our governments-not only the Liberal administration of to-day but other administrations in days gone by-seem to have listened to the voice of the big business combines. They have sat at the megaphone and desired to hear their master's voice rather than the voice crying the needs of Canada as a nation.
Since an hon. member across the way interrupted to talk about oil, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the same situation has existed in respect to oil. The other morning we read in the newspaper that a huge oil development was taking place in northwest Canada. That announcement was made by United States army officials. I placed a few questions in that regard on the order paper, as Mr. Speaker likes us to do, and what sort of answers did I get? I asked:
1.	Is there any portion of country in Canada's northwest which is under the control of the United States army, and if so, what portion of territory, and what are the boundaries?
The answer was:
There is no portion of Canadian territory under control of the United States army.
I think there is a technicality here by reason of which the government does not have to answer, yes.
2.	Is there any war-time oil development taking place in the Fort Norman area. . . .
The answer to that part of the second question was in the affirmative; in other words, yes; there is an oil development going on there. Then I went on to ask:
. . . and if so, how many oil wells are being drilled, and is such development being done under Canadian or American military authorities?
The answer was:
It is not in the public interest that the number of wells should be disclosed. The project is being carried out by the United States army with Canadian approval and cooperation.

War Appropriation-Labour
Like other members of the house I become nauseated at times when the government persists in saying that it is not in the public interest to reveal this or that. I see no reason why the Canadian people should not know the extent of the oil development being carried on in the Canadian northwest, but the Prime Minister says it is not in the public interest for them to know. I think it would be a little more to the point if the answer had been:
It is not in the interests of the Liberal party for us to tell the country. Then I asked:
3.	Is a pipeline being constructed in any part of this territory, and if so, is this being done under control of Canadian or American military-officials ?
The answer was:
The construction of a pipeline is part of the project mentioned in the answer to No. 2.
4.	If a pipeline is being built, what is the extent of this pipeline?
The answer was:
It would not be in the public interest to answer this question.
They do not want to tell us if the pipeline is three miles or three thousand miles.
5.	If war-time oil development is taking place in this territory, is equipment and men being supplied by Canadian or American authorities?
The answer was:
Both.
6.	To whom or what firms have the oil rights been sold or leased in this territory?
Well, they open up here just a little. This is the answer:
For many years the Northwest Company, a subsidiary of Imperial Oil Limited, held five leases and one permit obtained under departmental regulations authorized from time to time by order in council. The wells on these have been producing oil supplies for use in the Northwest Territories. These leases and permit now stand in the name of Imperial Oil Limited and that company has obtained thirty-six permits under regulations authorized by order in council P.C. 742, dated January 28, 1943.
To me it seems strange that it should take a Pearl Harbor to bring the United States authorities to explore the wealth of this nation while we could not get any development done in order to supply our own country with oil and gasoline in this emergency. Of course it is no secret; the United States military authorities are doing this work to save themselves, and incidentally we are letting them do it to save ourselves. But what have governments been thinking about in bygone years, that these vast reserves have not been developed for our own use?
Let us get back to the coal mining industry. I believe there are three essential needs to be kept in mind in endeavouring to find a solution of this coal mining emergency. The
first is that there should be made available sufficient man-power to man these mines. I do not think I need to elaborate on that point; the minister recognizes the importance of it. A second very important point in the solution of our national coal problem to-day, as I see it, is that there should be an orderly and adequate supply of necessary new equipment for the purpose of expanding our coal mining industry, if possible. I should like to say just a word about that. Last night I asked the Minister of Munitions and Supply if he had subsidized any coal mining industries in order that they might expand their plants. His reply was in the negative, but he went on to say that if any coal mining industry thought it could expand its plants, he would be the first to help it, and he would not let finance stand in his way, that it would have his assistance in doing so. Well, I was very glad to hear that statement, so that I asked the minister what procedure it would be necessary to follow. His reply was, "Just let the secretary of the coal mining company write the emergency coal production board." That is all right Mr. Chairman; but once again, as you see, the coal mining industry has to take the initiative; some secretary has to do it. Surely, if there is a fuel emergency in Canada, the government must accept some little responsibility in taking the initiative in that regard. These coal mining companies may or may not make application, but while they are making application, that does not help solve the immediate problem. Some expert has to go out; some engineer has to survey. They have to make their report. The matter must go through the various channels of red tape, and perhaps this coal mining company will be able to expand a little next fall, or a couple of years afterwards, I do not know when. Certainly something should be done immediately to increase the output of coal in Canada, if that is possible. Let us remember that there must be a time lag in this. The coal mining industry in Canada is not equipped- to put out more coal. In fact, if anything, its coal mining equipment is wearing out.
Another thing is that it must be remembered that the coal mining industry of Canada just cannot perform miracles. There is a third important matter in connection with the solution of the national coal emergency, namely, the* matter of distribution. I refer to a proper, adequate and orderly distribution of coal throughout Canada. I am told that today some shipments of coal are left unloaded in coal dealers' yards. Why? Because manpower cannot be obtained to do the unloading. Yard staffs are being depleted. There may be
War Appropriation-Labour

a man-power situation right there. Demurrage is charged on cars of coal left loaded. Undoubtedly delivery trucks are idle because there is not the man-power required for their operation. All these matters may seem tiny; nevertheless I suggest to the minister that the orderly distribution of coal should form part of the national coal policy of the country. Not only should the coal be got out, and not only should the men be put to work, but there should be supervision to see that it is adequately distributed, so that no city, town or hamlet will go cold this winter.
Before taking my seat I would say that there should be a little more coordination among government departments. When it comes to the man-power problem, as it affects coal mining, I am quite certain one could discover that there is not sufficient coordination among the three defence departments on the one hand, and the Department of Labour on the other, under which the national mobilization board operates. I have a point in mind which leads me to that belief. This is the case of a man who, although in the army, has certain deficiencies which prevent his going overseas. He is serving in what is known as the disposal corps.
I am not sure that I know the functions of that corps, but I would fancy it is sort of a clean-up organization. This man is a coal
miner,	holding his first-class papers. He applied for leave of absence to go back to the coal
mines.	I have regarded this case as a legitimate one, because the man in question had an elderly widowed mother who was in ill health and living alone. His home and that of his mother was in a coal mining town. This man had received a number of leaves of absence. He had gone back to the coal mines, and each time his leave expired he made his report. On a number of occasions leave was extended. This condition obtained until about six weeks ago, at which time, so I am informed, the national resources mobilization board recommended to the Department of National Defence that his request for leave to return to the coal mines be not granted. The result was that he was returned to the army, and so far as I know he is still there.
But what happened? Within a couple of weeks of the refusal of this man's application to return to the mines, the Prime Minister ran to the microphone or to the press announcing a national coal emergency in Canada. Sufely, if it were known to some members of the government that within a few days or weeks we would reach the stage where a national coal emergency would be declared, then all departments of government should have known about it. Surely the mobilization board should 
have known, and a recommendation of that kind should not have been made. This leads me to believe that there is not proper coordination among various departments of government in respect of this matter.
I close by taking just a little legitimate credit to this group, for the stand with respect to man-power it has taken in the past. This is the one group in the House of Commons that has had some foresight, even dating back to pre-war days-and it is the only one. This group has never had to retrace its steps. We have never had to change our policy.
You never had one.

We shall not have to
retrace our steps, and we shall not have to change our policy, because we know where we are going.
You never had a policy.
Hon. members across the way may laugh-
No wonder.
(Maisonneuve-Rosemont): If we laugh it is because we do not want to cry.

The hon. member who might be known as Count Haw-Haw, might haw-haw a little bit. Well, let him haw-haw about some of the things I shall say. It was only a few years ago that this group advised the government it was possible for the country to provide large sums of money.
Twenty-five dollars a month?

What did my hon. friend
say?
Twenty-five dollars a month?

Yes, twenty-five dollars a month. Mr. Chairman, my hon. friends who cry out in that way should wake up to the fact that we are supplying dozens of times twenty-five dollars a month, and we are supplying it, not to feed the people or to build their homes, but to make munitions of war, necessary as they are, to be sunk to the bottom of the ocean, or blown into the air.
I say to my hon. friends that if it can be done for that, why can it not be done to bring Canada to a place where she will have developed a really Canadian civilization. Instead of that, what did we do?
Talk!

I will tell you what the government should do; they should hang

War Appropriation-Labour
three brass balls on the top of the peace tower, so that people who pass by may know that we have been put in pawn to the rest of the world! That is what we had better do. We said we could issue money. The government is now doing it. They cried out, "Inflation!" We told them they could handle inflation, by a proper system of price control. "No, no!" said the Minister of Finance, "I will never stand for price control in Canada!" Within a year after he had risen in his place and said that they put in price control. That is what we told them they would have to do, and they did it. We told them they should subsidize industry, and what are they doing to-day? They are subsidizing industry by the hundreds and by the millions of dollars.
We said there should be a total war.
When the war broke out we said that we should not fool ourselves, that this war would be a long one, that we had better organize for total war.
Nobody knew where the money was coming from.
The Prime Minister of Canada was more interested in winning elections than he was in winning the war.
Oh, nonsense.

My hon. friend may say, "Oh, nonsense," but anyone that keeps half an eye open can see what has happened in Canada to-day. I knew that as soon as this group took a little credit for what it advised the government it would have to do, the pill would be too bitter for some private Liberal members to swallow.
It certainly would.

I am going to ask the minister to answer this question, to give this country an adequate answer if he can. Is the national coal emergency problem being solved? How is it being solved in respect of manpower, increased output and adequate and equitable distribution of coal? Let us remember that within two or three months cold weather will be upon us and then, if this problem is not solved, it will be an emergency indeed.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of attention to the oration the minister delivered this afternoon, and I wish to compliment him upon his presentation. It was as comprehensive a survey of the department as it has been my pleasure to listen to since I have had the privilege of sitting
in this chamber. I say that regardless of the fact that the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), who is sitting behind the minister, also made some pertinent statements while he was Minister of Labour. I think he laid the founda- . tion for the job the minister did to-day. I am sorry I cannot agree with everything the minister said. I am not going to attempt at this time to discuss the many ramifications of his statement, but for a few minutes I should like to deal with one aspect of what he said.
I believe this is the problem which is causing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and his genial undersecretary the greatest amount of anxiety and is one they would like to solve. Whether they have the authority to put into operation the necessary measures to solve this problem successfully, is a matter that will have to be determined by themselves.
This evening the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) discussed briefly the question of union recognition, a matter in which I am particularly interested. This problem is perhaps in the same position to-day as far as solution is concerned as it was when I first heard it discussed in this house in 1940, except that it may be more complicated. Many of the things that have been done since the outbreak of war have caused considerable confusion, and the complicated machinery that has been set up has retarded any progress in the right direction. For a few moments I should like to take the minister back over the trail and to try to draw the picture as I see it and have seen it for the past three years.
Over the week-end I sat in as a spectator at a conference of some 550 delegates who represented the trades union movement of Ontario. They were attending this conference irrespective of their union affiliations, they represented the C.I.O., the Canadian congress of labour and the A. F. of L. There was a unanimity of opinion because they had a common problem to solve. The thought that was uppermost in the minds of the delegates, section by section, was the establishment of industrial democracy. Democracy is not something that you can discuss in the abstract and let it go at that. We live in a democratic country; we are fighting for democracy and freedom; democracy is something that lives and must be exercised in the lives of the people in all phases of society. These men were discussing the industrial problems of Ontario, and they complained that democracy for the worker did not exist, regardless of all the platitudes the employers of Ontario have put out in advertising, in appeals to workers during victory bond campaigns and so forth.
War Appropriation-Labour

The Department of Labour is simply an instrument of the government to administer policy. I do not believe in pounding the minister or any other official of the department on account of the policy that is being administered. I think that is a wrong attitude to take. Any time I hear anyone saying that we should get rid of the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Finance, I always tell them to leave well enough alone, because every time that is done we generally get someone worse. They never make any improvement. What you must do is to change the policy that is being administered. If you do not do that, there is no use in bringing in someone else thinking he will do a better job.
Is the hon. member suggesting that the present minister is worse than the former one?

I leave that to the imagination of those who are listening. I am not going to make any accusations. I think the initial mistake that was made was to pass order in council 2685, which in very clear language gave the workers the right to organize. That order in council was nicely written, and it is a credit to the Secretary of State since it was during his regime that it was passed. It contained very nice language.
I helped to write it.

The minister did a very good job. The mistake that was made in passing this order in council, as well as the other
35,000	orders in council that have been passed since the outbreak of war, was that it was not given legal status. It should not have been left simply as a declaration of policy because it created the impression in the minds of the workers across the country that they had the right to go out and establish collective bargaining based on that order. By giving that order legal status; by making it mandatory, I think you would go a long way toward solving the problem with which we are confronted at the present time.
I have said on many occasions that since the outbreak of the war I did not think there had been a strike in this country where the workers had gone out because they had any desire to participate in a strike. I do not want to go through them all and thresh old straw but if you start off with Kirkland Lake and go on from there and examine all the representations that have been made and travel the road followed by the workers since, you will find that the legislation was the determining factor in bringing about the strike at Kirkland Lake. Although that strike took

place two years ago, I think it is not too late to .point out that if the employers at Kirkland Lake were as loyal as the workers to the interests of this country and had. recognized their responsibility in this serious war situation, there would have been no strike there. The government had appointed a commission headed by the man who now heads the national war labour board, M<r. Justice McTague, and that commission brought in a unanimous report recommending the miners' and smelters' union as the bargaining agency. But the employers at Kirkland Lake defied the laws of Canada and paid absolutely no attention to a government appointed board whose findings were implementing P.C. 2685. That strike was not brought about because the workers wanted to participate in it; they were forced to strike because the employers refused to recognize the laws of Canada and the findings brought in by that government-appointed board. You can go all through the ,piece and you will find that the same situation prevails. There is a reason for it, and this is my own opinion. I honestly believe that the employers in this country are not thinking in terms of winning the war, as the workers are. They are working on a long-range programme, and they are more concerned with their position when this war is over than they are in forgetting their own immediate problems and making an allout effort to bring this war to a successful conclusion as speedily as possible.
I say that the orders in council which form the basis of the government's labour policy are not an accident. They are a formula upon which the employers are working to keep the workers in an unorganized state, so that the employers may be in a position when this war is over, to dictate the labour policy of this country. I am not going to make that statement without qualifying it.
When I use the word "formula" I mean this. The formula upon which company unions were built in the United States for example, has been summed up in a very short sentence, as follows:
The fastest way to retard the growth of the trades union movement is to recognize it in principle, render it impotent, and do not allow it to function, and it will die of its own volition.
That formula is recognized in principle in P.C. 2685, which was followed by P.C. 7440, which partly tied up bargaining rights and restricted the right which had been exercise-able by unions prior to its passage. That order in council was followed by P.C. 8253.

By P.C. 5963.

War Appropriation-Labour

No; P.C. 8253 followed
P.C. 7440, and it further extended the restrictions. set up the bonus, and froze all wages at pre-war levels. That was not accidental. These things were well thought out by the heads of certain industries who exercise influence on certain boards. I said I was expressing my own opinion, but my analysis,
I believe, is based on common sense. I think that order in council was designed to keep wages at their pre-war level, so that they will be at that level when the war is over. That is the position the employers want to be in. The order in council means that the bonus goes off as soon as the war is over, but no one has passed an order in council saying that the cost of living will go back to pre-war levels when the war is over. Those wage rates are wage rates that should not be frozen upon any country. That order in council, P.C. 8253, after people had got used to it, slowly but surely prepared the minds of the industrial workers for what I term dictatorship, because when you get persons to accept direction from a certain quarter over a period of time, they gradually cease to struggle against it. The employers of this country realize that from an organization point of view the Canadian workers are in a very weak position. Perhaps only sixteen'per cent of those who are eligible for membership in trades unions actually belong to a union to-day.
Then they reached their arm in and took control over the franchise within the unions in P.C. 7307. I am not blaming the minister for the passage of these orders in council. My accusation is that the influence of the employers was sufficiently strong to have this formula worked out and passed along to someone who administers it. The government, of course, in the final analysis must bear the responsibility. Under P.C. 7307 the Minister of Labour has the right to determine how the vote shall be taken, who shall vote, how the vote shall be counted and scrutinized. There is only one instance that I know of where that power was exercised in a way that was detrimental to the best interests of the workers and to peace, order and good government in the section of the country concerned, and that was in Kirkland Lake, where that privilege was absolutely abused. I am not saying that it has been done since. What I am trying to point out is that every privilege and every right that the unions had under the laws of democracy has been usurped.
Then, of course, section 502A of the criminal code is supposed to give the workers a certain protection against discrimination. I am not a lawyer, but I have seen this issue tried in
the courts and it is impossible to get a conviction against an employer under section 502A. So that there is no protection there.
That formula has destroyed a very important section of organized society, the working people of this country. It is that formula against which I am trying to warn the people of Canada, because once you get a dictatorship over one section of society it is reflected sooner or later on every section. When you allow the liberties of one section of society to be taken away from them unfairly, it is not long before your own turn comes and you travel the same road. The formula that established company unionism I see clearly pictured in these five basic orders in council which frame the policy of the department. Any time the workers have a problem and appeal to the department, the department must take them through that formula. The net result is that frustration and delay occur, and later on the men walk off the job. Nothing else can happen. The steel walk-out was on that basis. After twenty months of negotiations; after travelling through all that machinery, the men went on strike. There is a situation now in Galt, Ontario, which has not yet been settled. Perhaps there have been mistakes on both sides. Nevertheless,, there is a serious interruption of work and a clash there.
The machinery as it exists at the present time makes it impossible to settle the matter, unless someone is big enough to exercise common sense and to say what is the solution of that problem. The solution of that problem is the exercise of democracy, the taking of a vote. That is the answer, and any employer who is not prepared tp accept that principle and to give the workers the privilege of voting on that question is not a democrat and does not believe in the exercise of democracy. I do not care about tags; I do not care what tag they give me-C.I.O., A.F. of L., or Canadian congress of labour. John L. Lewis has taken us around by the ears so much that I do not know' where we stand on these things. I sometimes think I am in the middle of the road, but it is immaterial to me. It is the principles of the organization that I stand for, and regardless of these tags that are hung upon them, the rank and file of the workers in any section of industry, in any of these organizations, are all fighting for the same thing, the right to the means of livelihood. Where there is a jurisdictional dispute I would be prepared to take exactly the same attitude with them as with the employers: You fellows cannot agree among yourselves. Fine. We will take a vote and settle this thing, and it will be settled on the same basis as that on which you elect
War Appropriation-Labour

your members of parliament and other representatives in other departments of organized society. No favouritism. That is exactly the basis on which it should be done. It is simple; it is plain; there is nothing to it. Take this Galt business. I have gone over the reports, both majority and minority reports, and I listened to the discussion on Sunday. It was focussed on that very question, and I think the Department of Labour should take immediate steps to see that the situation is handled in that way.
I am a little bit afraid of the way in which things are going. Labour is not making progress. You are facing a bad situation. The Minister of Munitions and Supply said about a month ago that they were changing their lines of production and that there would be interruption in plant after plant, retooling plants, and considerable unemployment for the next three or four months-that was his statement-and in the meantime, where you throw people from one section of industry to another and attempt to route them around, in an unorganized state, you have a problem on your hands.
The greatest asset you can have is to have your organization set up properly. Suppose you want to change a steel plant in Sydney to-morrow or over at the Sault. Your shortest cut and fastest way of doing the job is to get in touch with the union officials. They will do the job more effectively than anyone else I knojv of. But when you tackle a plant that has no organization, where the workers mill around in any direction, and you send a selective service officer in there, or an official from the labour department, to make that transfer or change, then you have a problem which it will take a long time to solve. You have suspicion and lack of direction. People do not want to move, and there is no direction. But that does not exist where workers are organized. Look at Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain. Why, collective bargaining is considered just as necessary to those countries as the functioning of our parliament here to-day is to us. It is part of the parliamentary set-up of those countries, and it is utilized to the fullest extent. I cannot understand, therefore, except for one reason, why the employers of Canada take the attitude they do in keeping their workers unorganized. There is only one answer, and it is this: I will get as much as I can during the process of winning the war. We will establish our controls in behind the scenes. We frame the policy upon which the workers will be kept disorganized, and when the war is over

we shall be in a position to control not only from the top but from the bottom, through the medium of plant council, superintendents and so forth, and the workers are not going to share in the democracy that we are fighting for overseas to-day. I know the minister is thinking about this. He is a trades unionist of long standing, and he realizes the significance of what I am saying on this question of the right of workers to sit around a conference table and to elect an agent who will sell their labour power to the boss. He said it was fundamental; that it was part of the set-up. Well, then, give legal status to order in Council P.C. 2685 and proclaim it and say that it must be accepted, otherwise there is a violation of the laws of the country. If it can be done with all the other orders in council that have been passed, it can be done with this one. Eliminate these disputes from all sections of the country These men want to elect someone to sell their labour power.
While I am on that subject, the Commercial Intelligence Journal of June 5 had an article from which I should like to quote. In New Zealand it is part of their regular set-up, part of their employment articles, part of their selective service regulations to recognize trade unions. I quote:
Employers in essential industries must notify tile district man-power officer of the names and addresses of all new workers. They are relieved of the responsibility, however, of ascertaining whether a man is a member of a trade union before engaging him. Now all workers in essential industries are to be considered members of an appropriate trade union and notifications to the man-power officers of names of new workers will be accessible to trade union secretaries. If a worker does not pay his trade union membership fee after reasonable requests it may be deducted from his pay.
Those are instructions right from the government to their selective service officers.
Mr. MITCHELL; One has to be a member by law.

That is what I am pointing out, and I think the same thing should apply to Canada.
There is another point I wish to make and I am not saying this for the purpose of arguing with the minister. The minister said this afternoon that within his department labour had representatives on practically every section of the department, administering regulations. That may be true. They may have representatives sitting in; I am not quarrelling with that; but they are not on the basis where they can be considered as representing the viewpoint, the hopes and the aspirations of the organizations

War Appropriation-Labour
that sent them there. They are there in an administrative capacity or in an advisory capacity. They have no say in the making of the law. That is the point I want to make.

I do not wish to interrupt, but the governor in council and this chamber are the only people who can make the laws. That is fundamental. First of all, you have to be elected, and then of course you have to be called into the government. You have to have the two agencies. I know of no country where an individual belonging to an organization, whether it be employers or employees or farmers, fashions the laws. All they do is merely to advise. The final responsibility for the safety of the state must be with the government and this parliament.

Yes; I agree with that. The minister says he does not know of any country in the world where the laws are made except by members of parliament and the government itself. We are living in one where that is done, right in Canada. That is exactly what I am quarrelling with. Your orders in council that are being passed have the same effect as the statute laws and are not drafted by the Minister of Labour or by any other minister, and they do not come before this parliament for ratification. Your emergency fuel production board formulates laws that will govern the producing of coal; and so on through each department. Your labour representatives are not given that privilege. Industry have their representatives in framing these orders in council.
Not as far as my department is concerned.

I am not now arguing with the minister; I do not know. But I am saying that labour is in an unfortunate position from the viewpoint of having any influence in the making of orders in council or of the laws, of having any opportunity of representing their people on that basis. They merely sit in and take whatever laws are framed by the department or its advisers, and they are placed in the position of having to go out and sell something to the workers of this country which they have no voice in determining. In Great Britain the trade union congress officials sit right in with the war boards which formulate war labour policies. Unless the representatives of labour in Canada can perform a similar function, I certainly would not want to be sent by my organization to take a position in the minister's department and have to justify existing orders in council which regulate labour affairs. The minister has many good men in
his department, but these men are placed in a rather impossible position. They are trying to make something work which is not workable, and they are in a sorry position when they face their organizations with a proposition of that kind. Until these fellows are given some opportunity of guiding those who are making the laws through order in council or otherwise, I do not think it can be said that labour has representation on any board that functions, since it has no say in the making of the laws.
Another matter: in making appointments the minister consults with the heads of the congresses, and persons are recommended by these bodies, but when they are taken in here and given a job on a board they are no longer responsible to their organizations. The organization has absolutely nothing to say as to the appointee's activities on the board; yet he has some responsibility to his union. These men should have at least sufficient freedom to give an account of their stewardship to their organizations.

Is not the policy of
which my hon. friend speaks the policy as far as the British trades union congresses are concerned?
They go back to their congress.
Oh, no.
Oh, yes; they do.

I know whereof I speak. I have gone into that thoroughly; I have also gone into the other matters which my hon. friend has been discussing this evening. With a lot that he has said I agree. But any outside organization cannot in the very nature of things, * under a democratic form of government, be responsible for the fashioning of the laws; that is the responsibility of the government and parliament. This principle is elementary. I know the official attitude of the British trades union congress toward this matter. They send in a panel to the government, and the government picks out the members they want. The final authority is the government; they pick out the member they want on a particular board. From then on he is a free agent. I know what is in my hon. friend's mind. He has the United States viewpoint, with their international trades union movement. Like myself, he was raised in the international trades union movement and probably he has that North American viewpoint. When one talks about compulsory bargaining in Great Britain, my hon. friend knows there is no legal basis for a trade union in Great Britain such as there is in the United States.
War Appropriation-Labour

I understand that. I am not arguing that point. The point I am making is that the British trades union congress have a policy. They have a policy with respect to this war; and when they send Sir Walter Citrine or anyone else to the government with a proposal for the enactment of certain laws or certain policies, he comes back and reports to the congress.
That is, as a delegation.
No; they have permanent officials sitting in.
I know whereof I speak.

They have permanent officials sitting in framing policies. Bevin is still responsible to his organization. Not so long ago he had some difficulty in justifying certain things which he was instrumental in bringing into the House of Commons. He is still responsible to his organization. These men are not cut adrift.

I am not going to argue. This is like being in a local union meeting. But if I might put it in this way, my hon. friend is not responsible to the United Mine Workers of America because he, being a member of them, is a member of the House of Commons. I am a member of the International Union of Operating Engineers, but as minister of the crown I am not responsible to that organization. It just does not add up.

I think you are. I think, as members of the trades union movement, both yourself and myself are morally responsible in this house and out of this house to live up to the principles, policies and obligations of our organizations.
That is another matter entirely.

No; it is not another matter entirely. I keep closely in touch with what my union is doing, and they keep closely in touch with what I am doing, and any time I rise in my place in the house to make a pronouncement on that industry I am absolutely certain that what I am saying is in accordance with their policy. I hope I shall always retain that loyalty and recognition of the principles of the people who sent me here.

That is different
altogether.

In my opinion, when a member of a trades union movement gets away from that principle, he is slipping as far as the movement is concerned.

But I am not going to argue that point. The point I wanted to make was that labour, in my opinion, has no representation on these boards. I look upon them as merely, I do not want to say apologists, for legislation for which they are not responsible. Unless they are privileged to sit in with the minister or with those who are framing orders in council and have at least some recognition or have included in the regulations some of the principles which the organized movement supports, they cannot morally go out and support legislation which completely nullifies the whole work of the movement.
Under order in council P.'C. 5963 the cost of living bonus needs, I think, reexamination. I know the minister is well aware of the fact that it is not uniform, and I do not believe it is possible to establish in Canada from one coast to the other a satisfactory cost of living bonus based on the figures compiled by the bureau of statistics. I think wrhat the minister will have to do is to have a regional cost of living bonus arrangement set up, and when his board is determining wages in a certain section, the cost of living index as applicable to that particular section is the one on which it should base its findings when recommending a cost of living bonus. Go to the eastern end of Nova Scotia and compare the cost of living since the outbreak of war with -what it is here or in certain sections of Ontario, and you will find a great discrepancy. The index as handed out by the bureau of statistics is certainly not applicable to that section of the country.
With respect to labour management committees, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East that the Department of Labour has missed the boat in not establishing national industrial councils for every section of industry in Canada, as exemplified by the building industiy. That was done early in the war; it has worked out satisfactorily, and there has been little difficulty in that industry. I think the same thing would apply in any branch of industry if they were granted the right of organization-the building industry is organized

and if you had a national council set up, so that you could call in representatives of the unions and of the employers and work out formulas in connection with the re-tooling of plants and the transfer from one kind of production to another. That would be a wonderful thing to have to-day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The present minister was the organizer of that construction council.

I know that, and it is unfortunate that it was not done in every industry. If we could call in representatives

War Appropriation-Labour
of the employers and of labour in the steel industry, for example to work out plans for the re-tooling of plants, the shuffling of employees to other lines of work necessary to the war effort, and so on, it would certainly facilitate the work of the selective service officials.
The hon. member for Macleod spoke at some length on the fuel situation. I am not going to discuss that matter to-night because I went into it to a certain extent with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I gave him my opinions; I told him what I thought was wrong and what I thought would have to be done to meet the situation. I believe that matter is now entirely in the hands of Munitions and Supply; the Department of Labour has nothing to do with the emergency war production board, so that I am not going to discuss that problem now. However, I would urge the minister to use whatever influence he has in the cabinet to have legal status given to order in council P.C. 2685', and then I would urge that he use every means at his disposal to settle the trouble at Galt. As I saw that situation on Sunday, it may develop into a very difficult matter to handle; many things may happen in connection with it. It is not good enough to say this side was wrong, or that side was wrong. Perhaps both sides were wrong; but still the problem exists; people are suffering who should be working and producing, and the war effort is suffering. Every effort should be made by the Department of Labour to settle the difficulty. It is an unfortunate situation, and the solution is so simple that it is hard to understand why such a situation should be allowed to continue. So that I would urge the minister to do what he can to settle that dispute. Then if he has any influence with national selective service and with the Department of Munitions and Supply, I urge him to exercise that influence to the end that the 289 men who were discharged from the Toronto shipyards and who, in my opinion, were dismissed illegally by their, employer, without consultation with selective service, may be put back at work as key men in a key industry at this time.

I have read with considerable interest the statements the minister had placed on our desks this evening, and I should like some further information with regard to this summary of mobilization statistics. I think it is somewhat misleading to term this information statistics. For example, the summary states:
The difference of approximately 380,000 between the number of men sent notices-medieal, and the number examined is accounted for by
notices undelivered, men who joined the forces voluntarily either before or on receiving notice-medical, men sent notices to whom the regulations do not apply, and some defaulters. Men registered from January to March 15, 1943, as not receiving notice-medical narrows the difference between notices sent and men examined. But without doubt voluntary enlistments account for a very substantial portion of the total difference. '
Then it goes on:
The reduction of approximately 319,000 in the number called for military training, compared to the number examined, is accounted for by men being medically unfit, men being granted postponements-and again (but no doubt fewer in number) voluntary enlistments. Defaulters would also add to the difference.
I think we should have some further information with regard to the difference of 380,000. A national registration was taken in 1940, when the people in all parts of Canada cooperated generously to give the government the information that was desired, and very large amounts of public money have been expended in maintaining the services. It seems hardly possible that 380,000 men could be notified to report for medical examination without some more definite information as to why they did not report. For example, I think we should know how many defaulters there were in the 380,000. I should like the minister particularly to give information as to the number of notices sent to men who at the time had been reported killed in action. I have had one case of this kind brought to my attention, and several hon. members have spoken about the same matter. There was one case of an airman who was reported missing and presumed dead. After his mother had received this sad information, a notice came to the home directing this young man to report for his medical examination. Would the minister give the committee the number
