speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Before the
minister answers, I should like the opinion of the committee, as it was obtained in connection with the other departments which have been under consideration. The committee seemed to be satisfied with the general discussion we had to-day, which no doubt will be carried on for the first one or two items to be called. I should like the consensus of the committee as to whether or not an item should be called now. I realize it will have to be done as it was done in the other departments. I believe the committee wishes to apply the same principle at the present time.

The minister made a general statement this afternoon, and he has given specific information. Before we proceed to the detailed discussion he should give us some additional information. That is why I raised the question to-night, so that we might have this information available when we come to this particular item.

A number of hon. members are not present to-night on account of an important dinner held in connection with the meetings of the parliamentary association. I am sure some hon. members would like to speak to this question, and I hope the matter will not be closed until they have the opportunity to say something.
I think we should leave the matter open.

To keep the discussion in order, I was going to suggest that I will get the information for which my hon. friend has asked in ample time for him to ask other questions. If, in the early part of the committee stage, we are to go on a roving commission, then we are likely to be here for a month. I thought that to-day and perhaps to-morrow certain members on both sides of the house would make statements. After that, many of the questions they have in the backs of their minds will come before the committee. Then I can have those questions looked into, and answers can be given the next day, the same as the other ministers have done. However, in my opinion it is unwise now to go on a roving commission. If we are to start with the estimates, we should keep them in order, commencing with this sheet, and following in sequence.
I agree with the hon. member for Haldimand that some hon. members on both sides of the house who would wish to make statements are not here to-night.

I believe it is agreed
that some hon. members who would like to make statements on the broad principles of the question are unavoidably absent. It might be well to leave the matter open until tomorrow. It would be well to proceed as we are now doing, and let any hon. member who wishes to speak to avail himself of the opportunity now offered.

This is a regular session
of the committee. I agree with the minister when he suggests that we ought to be prepared to go on with the items. If we are finished with the general discussion, we ought to be prepared to go on with the items as they appear. If members are absent, it is their own fault. They know the house is sitting to-night, and they should be here. Let us get on with the business of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As the committee
realizes, in respect of the other four departments much latitude had to be given in the first part of the discussion. I understand fully the point raised by the hon. member for Haldimand, when he states that some hon. members to-night are unavoidably absent. They cannot be blamed for that. It seems to me a majority in the committee wishes to follow a certain procedure. I have noticed that officials of departments have had to be brought in at different times to give necessary information to ministers, and that fact must make us realize how difficult it is for the minister to have at hand all the information required. I would assume, however, that there would be a general discussion allowed at least on the first two items before they are passed.

A number of hon. members on this side of the house did not know the house was meeting to-night, and I suggest we might as well rise and report progress. This man-power question is the most important matter with which we are faced. A discussion of two or three hours would clear up a great deal of misunderstanding.

I do not see why the
business of the house should be delayed because some hon. members wish to attend a dinner. That is not sufficient reason. If the business before the committee is of such great importance, why do they not attend the sittings, instead of a dinner? We must be reasonable in these matters. I should hope the fullest latitude would be given hon. members in this discussion.

Only three members of
the cabinet are in their seats to-night. They are just as much to blame as are private

War Appropriation-Labour
members. They were not told that if they were not here this debate would not go on. I noticed that the officials were being brought in, and I was going to say something about it. They should not have been brought in tonight. This matter cannot be rushed, because many hon. members will have something to say. I am not saying anything to-night, but I am going to see that those who1 do wish to speak will have some protection.
My hon. friend will probably agree that we are the finest parliamentary association in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I believe we should
carry on in the asking of questions and the making of statements.

I had not wished to take
part in this debate, but I can tell you this, that as one of the private members in the opposition I am very much surprised at the man-power policy of this government. I saw this war coming on in 1936, 1937 and 1938. I proposed that there should be a national selective service registration, because anyone who could read the signs of the times must have known that Canada would be involved in the war, and that the first thing required would be a national selective service register. That is something we had never had before. The first domesday book set out the population, and the available man-power between the ages of twenty-one and sixty. It is part and parcel of the assessment laws of the provinces and municipalities, and such a register should have been undertaken. This question came before the house on many occasions, but a selective service programme was not decided upon.
Then there was some consideration as to whether we should continue with the voluntary system under the Militia Act, or, in addition, have a compulsory system. When the war broke out, we found we had thrown away our army, navy and air force, and that to a great extent we were dependent upon the mother country for protection. I have no quarrel with the present minister at all. He has been trying to take up the load where others left off.
This government has never had a man-power policy. I remember the recruiting policy as it applied in Toronto shortly after the war broke out. Some of the young people walked in from Aurora and Newmarket, in the dead of winter -I believe the date was January 6, 1940- and landed at the armouries at Toronto. But the doors were not opened until after ten o'clock. The pictures of those young people
were put in the papers, and there was some discussion as to the way in which the manpower situation was being handled.
We have gone pretty far along that line when we announce the conscription of high school students between sixteen and eighteen years of age. We have gone a long way when we have brought them under the conscription regulations, because that is all it is. Some may not like the word, but the fact is that we have conscription in this country. We have conscription of man-power. What for? Well, we are told, it is for home defence. We know there is no such thing as home defence. The people in the invaded countries-Norway, Belgium, Denmark, Holland and France-found out there was no such thing as home defence against the axis powers. The government came along and said in an election campaign that as long as they were in power there would be no such thing as compulsory man-power. A vote was held on the policy and programme of the government as announced by the Prime Minister and other ministers of the crown during the election campaign.
What are the facts? We seem to be the only dominion which has been going on in this haphazard fashion, so far as the war and the question of man-power are concerned. I come from an industrial city, one which has made a magnificent contribution. Its supply of manpower was practically dried up from voluntary enlistments. Not only that, but young men from that city enlisted from points right across Canada. That became necessary on account of the arrangement whereby artillery units were formed in one province, infantry in another and air force in another. The result was that many Toronto citizens, and citizens of other cities in Ontario, enlisted at points from Halifax to Vancouver.
The Minister of Labour has a very able assistant in Mr. MacNamara. Mr. Mac-Namara cleaned up a very bad situation in connection with money for dependents, and he deserves {he thanks of the dependents of the soldiers who are fighting overseas to-day. I do not think the government have been fair with the people of Canada. Up to the last month there has been only one national seelctive industry in Canada, agriculture. About a month ago when the clamour rose for more fuel the government passed an order in council. I have known the Minister of Labour for many years, and he brought down a measure concerning the coal industry, making it the second national selective service industry.
They do not have this system of obtaining man-power in the air force or the navy
39SO
War Appropriation-Labour

because there has been a rush of men to those two services. In the army they have what is called voluntary service, and they have draftees for home defence. The work overseas is done largely by those who enlisted volnntarily. Then the home defence was widened to take in Bermuda and other territories in the Atlantic, as well as on the Pacific. I am very much disappointed in the *way in which the man-power problem has been handled. There has been no equality of service, nor has there been equality of sacrifice. There will be homes in Toronto where high school children of sixteen, seventeen and eighteen years of age will be taken away when the father is overseas and perhaps the mother in a munitions plant.
I have no personal quarrel with the minister or any other minister, as I have been a friend of his for a long time. But I say to him that he cannot succeed under the present belated system. I want to be fair to the government because I have known no politics since the war started. I have been ready to support the government if they had a total war effort, but they have not had that. I have seen how these recruiting units work around Toronto. It is a case of [DOT] on again, off again, on again. Then they went to work and put out a lot of advertising, they put up billboards and appointed citizens committees to aid recruiting. I am prepared to say that you might as well not spend any money on home defence because there is no such thing as home defence. We are continually going to Washington for ideas, but what did they do in that country? They put in the draft. Just shortly before Munich the Chamberlain government in Great Britain brought in a system of national selective service.
The programme of the minister is divided into a multiplicity of classifications, and I notice that there are many registers. The one register about which we heard so much was committed to the archives. It is a case of earth to earth, dust to dust and ashes to ashes. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud) is somewhat of a humorist, but I can remember when he and some of his colleagues seemed to be quite pleased that this report dealing with man-power was put in the archives. Everybody had to register and carry around his registration certificate. They even went into the restaurants, theatres and along the streets to ask men for their registration cards. I see a former mayor over there, a very fine citizen in his country who is nowr sitting behind the minister. I do not know whether he wras asked for his

registration card, but I have seen men hauled out of hockey matches and football games, and asked to show their cards.
You cannot fight Hitler with registrations. There are no labour unions in Germany; far from it. If the United States had a system like this, they would not have the army they have to-day. What is the policy of the government in connection with conscripting these sixteen, seventeen and eighteen-year-old youths? What is the policy of the government with respect to amateur and professional sport? The minister has failed to give this matter any attention. We should have a national policy with regard to sport in connection with the war. The present head of the Free French has said that there should not be a-glorification of sport in connection with war. The figures presented by the minister are just the opposite to what the government has said. The government said that there would be no conscription in any form. That is what they told the electors of this country; that is what they told the people of Toronto; that is what they told the people of my constituency - they were promised that there would be no such thing as compulsory registration.
Then we have a registration of retail and wholesale trade. Is aynone allowed to conduct business? He cannot with the present controls and subcontrols that are in force. We have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) saying one thing and other ministers saying other things in connection with national selective service. Mr. Chairman, you have proved to be very popular, and I am sure that if you had had anything to do with it, we would not have the present mixup.
Here is the Minister of Labour bringing down this programme to-day to send our high school population of sixteeen, seventeen and eighteen years of age out into the woods to cut trees while a lot of the government are away out at the country club. I do not know what hours they keep there, but there must be a very large attendance at the country club to-night. I see many seats in the house vacant. Probably a great many members have gone home. If this is the best programme the Minister of Labour can bring down, to draft our high school population of sixteen, seventeen and eighteen years to go out into the woods and chop down trees, for that is what they are going to do, that is a fine exhibition of national selective service. The dog days are here. A lot of members have gone fishing, or will be going soon. The minister is a popular sport. If he goes through some of the departments of the public service, he will find in one

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
department that over 5,976 officers in the air force who never knew how to form threes were put in uniform the next day and are now marching around the streets and in the department stores taking salutes. There is a large body of good sports on the government benches, many of whom have done good work in the municipal service of this country. I ask if they will rise in their places and say that they are in favour of the present form of conscription in this country. In the olden days it was declared by some of the leaders here that if war came we would have to have a national vote of the people before we could declare war. and one of our own leaders said it, too.
I look at this document which has been distributed among the members, entitled " Statistics on National Selective Service and Man-power." Statistics! That is all we have 'been getting. We have been fighting Germany on statistics all the time. There has been a regular carnival of statistics. In the early days of the war Britain did it. She dropped tons of literature on the cities and towns of Germany, and a great deal of it was written in the two great languages of this country.
My good friend beside me, the hon. member for Haldimand, seems very bashful to-night, and I see the young member for Fraser Valley in his place at the moment. A little while ago I saw him sitting in the seat of the Prime Minister and then he crossed the floor and sat in our leader's seat for a while.
I want to ask my friends to my left, and we have some good clergymen and good teachers among them, what do they think of this programme of sending our high school children, whose fathers are overseas, out into the woods to cut down timber?
I see magnificent parades around the city streets for victory loan, recruiting and national selective service. Last September there was a line up at 174 Spadina avenue of several thousand men and women to register at the selective service offices there, staffed by a lot of government-appointed officials with no war record. But if you want any kind of help you cannot get it from national selective service. A prominent citizen told me that as soon as he trains a man someone else calls him for something else. I never believed in this scheme of national selective service or in the government's handling of the whole manpower situation since the war began. I have lost all confidence in them. I believe in always telling the people the truth, especially during the war. I believe that one of the cardinal principles of good government is to keep people informed as to what goes on in
connection with the war. But the people have not been given the real facts of the man-power situation.
We have Mr. Donald Gordon. He has a man-power policy of his own. Does Gordon's department come under this programme of the minister? I can tell you, no, because he is a parliament in himself. The house of Gordon has assumed the powers and functions of the House of Commons and of the Senate too. It is eleven o'clock, I have not finished.
May I ask the minister or his assistant to make clear what items we shall be considering when we get to the stage of dealing with items?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: If hon. members will refer to Hansard of March 3 of the present year, they will find at the bottom of page 919 under the general title "Labour", the items which we shall follow in committee. The statement furnished to the members to-day is a further break-down of items in accordance with the practice laid down by the ministers of defence when they presented their estimates.

I wish a happy birthday to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
